Breaking: Elf Is A Holiday Classic Now, But One Star Admits It Was ‘Risky’ Business At The Time

  • According to recent reports, andy Richter, who played Morris in the Jon Favreau-directed comedy, recently reflected on the making of Elf and explained why the movie was considered something of a gamble.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, with the holiday season upon us and the 2026 movie calendar winding down, there are a handful of the best Christmas movies I return to every December, and Elf is pretty much guaranteed to make the list. Will Ferrell running around Fresh York City in yellow tights, eating spaghetti covered in candy and screaming about Santa Claus has become as much a part of the holidays as putting up the tree. According to one of the movie's stars, Hollywood wasn't exactly convinced it had a future Christmas classic on its hands back in 2003.

According to recent reports, andy Richter, who played Morris in the Jon Favreau-directed comedy, recently reflected on the making of Elf and explained why the movie was considered something of a gamble. Speaking with People while promoting his new book, Elf: Unwrapped, which he co-wrote with Aaron Karo, Richter said the movie's eventual success makes it easy to forget just how uncertain things were when production began.

It was a risky movie, and nobody thinks about that because it’s now a classic, but at the time there was nobody that was aching to make a movie with Will Ferrell as the star or with Jon Favreau as the director, for that matter.

Recent findings suggest that considering Will Ferrell himself had doubts when he first tried on Buddy's iconic costume, I can understand why some studio executives might have been nervous. At the time, the SNL alum was best known for his work on Saturday Night Live, where he'd spent seven seasons establishing himself as one of the show's biggest stars. He'd appeared in movies like Old School and Zoolander, but he hadn't yet proven he could carry a major studio comedy as its leading man.

It has been revealed that favreau, meanwhile, had directed the 2001 comedy Made, but he was still relatively inexperienced behind the camera. According to Richter, the studio was taking a chance on both men. He added:.

They were rolling the dice with this movie and it really paid off.

It's funny to think about now, considering Ferrell went on to become one of the biggest comedy stars of the 2000s, while Favreau would eventually direct Iron Man, helping launch the Marvel Cinematic Universe. He's also had a major hand in shaping the modern Star Wars franchise with The Mandalorian. But back in 2003, the idea of giving a relatively untested leading man a Christmas comedy about a grown man raised by elves probably sounded pretty ridiculous on paper. And considering some of the behind-the-scenes stories about making Elf, it's remarkable how well everything came together. It is a ridiculous premise. That's a big part of why I love it.

Richter also credited the combination of Ferrell's comedic instincts and Favreau's approach to storytelling for making the movie work. Interestingly, though, the movie’s star recently addressed the longstanding rumors about his relationship with Favreau during the production. It seems there's still plenty to learn about what went into making this particular Christmas classic. As for Richter, he told the outlet that the film succeeds because:.

The combination of their two sensibilities, which we go into in the book, that really made it work because it’s funny, but also has a lot of heart.

In a recent development, I think that's a pretty accurate assessment. Ferrell gets to be completely absurd as Buddy, whether he's congratulating a coffee shop for having the world's best cup of coffee or trying to navigate a revolving door. Yet the movie also gives us a genuinely sweet story about a guy looking for his father and trying to find somewhere he belongs.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

It has been revealed that james Caan's performance as Walter Hobbs deserves some credit here, too. His perpetually irritated reaction to Buddy's enthusiasm makes their relationship work, and without that dynamic, I don't think the movie would have nearly the same emotional payoff. Whatever reservations Hollywood had about the project, audiences certainly didn't share them once it arrived in theaters.

Industry observers note that according to The Numbers, Elf opened to more than $31 million during its first weekend in November 2003. It has since earned approximately $234 million worldwide, including revenue from subsequent theatrical releases. That's a pretty impressive return for a movie with a reported $32 million production budget.

The movie was successful enough that Hollywood naturally wanted another one, though Ferrell has since explained why he walked away from a potentially lucrative Elf sequel.

According to recent reports, more than two decades later, it's difficult to imagine the holiday season without Buddy the Elf. The movie remains a favorite among families, and people are still finding new things to appreciate about it, including one particularly interesting question about Buddy's journey from the North Pole to New York City.

I find it interesting that a movie nobody could guarantee would succeed has become something people practically schedule their Christmas celebrations around. Ferrell has made plenty of successful comedies since, and Favreau's career has gone places nobody could have predicted in 2003.

It has been revealed that there's something special about Elf. Considering how many Christmas movies come and go without making much of an impression, I suspect the people who took that gamble are pretty happy they did.

Elf is streaming with a Hulu subscription.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jen Affleck and her estranged husband, Zac Affleck, have revealed the sex of their fourth baby.

It has been revealed that in a sweet Instagram post uploaded on Thursday, November 26, Jen, 27, Zac, 30, and their three kids got involved in the beach picnic gender reveal. (Jen and Zac are already parents to daughters Nora, 5, and Penelope, 16 months, and son Luca, 3.).

The family cut into a cake with wine glasses, revealing that Jen and Zac are expecting another daughter.

“Our story may be changing, but the love we have for our babies never will. 🤍we love you baby girl,” the caption accompanying the post read.

Industry observers note that jen unveiled in June that the pair were expanding their family by sharing a carousel of photos where she highlighted off her baby bump. “Chapter Four. 🤍,” the Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star wrote alongside the post.

Months later, the duo dropped the bombshell that they had split, with Jen filing for divorce on November 3 after seven years of marriage.

Jen exclusively told Us on November 10 that her pregnancy was one of the catalysts that led her to choose to end her marriage, insisting that “the same reason why I filed for divorce is the same reason why it was really hard.”.

“It was this fourth child. I had to ask myself very hard questions like, ‘Is this the type of relationship I want this child to look up to?’” she told Us. “When I realized it was a no, that’s when I realized that I needed to make a change. You’ll see a lot of that unfold in season [1 of the Orange County spinoff].”.

Jen explained that filming Mormon Wives put a magnifying glass on a lot of her marital problems as well, accelerating the decision to leave the relationship.

According to recent reports, “I think doing reality TV for sure sped up the process [of calling it quits] because when you’re filming and you’re rewatching your life unfold in front of millions of people, it’s the difference between looking in a mirror,” she continued. “It highlights things.”.

After their separation was made public, Zac posted a TikTok video addressing the split and admitting to “mistakes.”.

“I don’t want anyone speaking bad about Jen, I don’t. I’ll just be the first to say I’ve made plenty of mistakes in our marriage, and it just really was time for us to go our own ways,” Zac remarked via the post on November 5. “We got married so young, and it sucks because I really did feel like we had something pretty special when we got married, but life happened. We had four kids. We signed up for reality TV on a show that’s really hurt a lot of people’s lives.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that PC modders are racing to get GTA 6 playable on PC after the leak of the game's complete Xbox build, but so far it doesn't look too promising.
  • PC modders are racing to get GTA 6 playable on PC after the leak of the game's complete Xbox build, but so far it doesn't look too promising.
  • GTA 6 publisher Take-Two Interactive and developer Rockstar Games haven't been sitting idle either, as one of the leads behind the Project Leonida Discord group claimed in now-deleted social media posts that they were stepping away from the mammoth task of getting GTA 6 to run on PC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that PC modders are racing to get GTA 6 playable on PC after the leak of the game's complete Xbox build, but so far it doesn't look too promising. GTA 6 publisher Take-Two Interactive and developer Rockstar Games haven't been sitting idle either, as one of the leads behind the Project Leonida Discord group claimed in now-deleted social media posts that they were stepping away from the mammoth task of getting GTA 6 to run on PC. Project Leonida has also been taken down, but it's not the only group trying to get GTA 6 running outside of PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ble-JJxBBGA None of these groups have succeeded yet, and as Twitter user Chasm detailed online, maybe relying heavily on AI tools isn't the way to go. Dev streams have been full of owners leveraging generative AI tools to do something, with several prompts being absolute gems of wishful thinking. Here's a snippet of what people have been throwing at Google's Antigravity, while butchering the English language: Continue working and do apply ever part of the code make no mistakes You need todo one thing at a time not a little bit of everything we need all the game start like the rockstar launch so on that stuff, not in game stuff yet work faster there has to be a faster way to iterate than this Even with an army of enthusiasts throwing prompts and cash at generative AI, a copied version of GTA 6 still seems far out of reach. Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick commented in March that the idea of using AI and simply pushing a button to make a hit game was "laughable," and he referenced the music industry, which is grappling with a flood of AI slop to top streaming platforms. "Right now [in music] there are programs that allow you to put out a prompt and get a professionally recorded song spit back out at you. It sounds like a song, but I defy you to listen to it more than once. It's great to send as a greeting card to your partner on their birthday, but that's about it," Zelnick said. Whatever progress is made in the GTA 6 PC port scene, don't expect it to last long before Take-Two's lawyers pounce. The publisher hasn't shied away from protecting its IP in the past, and takedown notices for any future GTA 6-related projects seem likely. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I write a lot about e-readers and e-ink tablets for Lifehacker, and one matter I'm constantly grappling with is how to write informatively about a bunch of devices that can be quite different in some details, like build or native firmware, and pretty much identical in others, given that literally all e-ink devices use display technology produced by the same Chinese tech giant. (It's called E-Ink.) The best way to do this is to include more video in my articles, but I've lacked a good way to film hands-free so I can easily demonstrate a device's look and feel—until recently.

I recently got an offer to try out a magnetic neck mount from Telesin, a low-cost option to turn my iPhone into a wearable so I can keep my hands free while filming. It's a pretty basic concept, but well-executed: The band that goes around your neck is made of rubber with a firm but flexible core, so you can easily position it to be longer or shorter or at an angle, and the phone mount is on an extending arm with three joints to give you additional options.

It has been revealed that I haven't had a chance to film anything for public consumption quite yet, but my testing has already given me some great ideas for how I can use it to show off, say, what it's really like to use a micro-reader in comparison to a full-sized Kindle, as I'll be able to wear it to give a more accurate user's point of view. And right now is a good time to pick one of them up, as many of Telesin's phone and camera accessories (including similar models built to handle an action camera like a GoPro) are discounted for Black Friday; the one I tested is down to $17, or 15% off.

This won't be the right device for every filming scenario. Though MagSafe holds my iPhone fairly securely, I found that I would accidentally detach it every time I tried to adjust the shooting angle—once even leading me to drop it. That's potentially bad news, as using it may require you to take the phone out of its case if it isn't MagSafe-compatible. (Mine isn't.) But if you're just looking for an inexpensive way to shoot hands-free video in a controlled environment, it could be exactly what you need.

Blade Runner 2099 Proves The Saga Does One Thing Better Than Any Other Sci-Fi Franchise

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that continuing the legacy of two of the greatest sci-fi movies ever made is a major enough challenge.
  • Recent findings suggest that it's hard to imagine, but "Blade Runner" had a tiny VFX budget.
  • In a recent development, as such, when Denis Villeneuve managed to both emulate the feel of Scott's classic and push the production design in new directions with "Blade Runner 2049," it was nothing short of a miracle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that continuing the legacy of two of the greatest sci-fi movies ever made is a major enough challenge. Doing so on the small screen adds an extra element of difficulty. Incredibly, "Blade Runner 2099" has overcome the odds to deliver yet another intoxicating excursion into the techno-industrial urban decay-scape so magically realized back in 1982's "Blade Runner" and so faithfully recreated in 2017's "Blade Runner 2049." As such, the Blade Runner franchise is now surely the most consistent on-screen sci-fi saga ever made. (Setting aside sci-fi sagas that are directed by the same person the whole time, like James Cameron's "Avatar.").

Recent findings suggest that it's hard to imagine, but "Blade Runner" had a tiny VFX budget. Yet director Ridley Scott and his production team managed to create one of the most believable and immersive worlds in cinema history. The famous "Hades" opening shot immediately plunges you into a future post-ecological collapse, in which technology seems to have almost grown on the wreckage of a fallen world like moss on fallen trees. The debris of society is adorned with neon and machinery, creating an environment in which past and future collide. "Blade Runner" might have been buried at the box office by "E.T. The Extra-Terrestrial," but it was an absolutely enthralling sci-fi adventure that came to define the genre.

In a recent development, as such, when Denis Villeneuve managed to both emulate the feel of Scott's classic and push the production design in new directions with "Blade Runner 2049," it was nothing short of a miracle. The "Dune" director's take on the world first introduced to audiences in 1982 was immediately familiar as the same one in which Harrison Ford's Rick Deckard did battle with Rutger Hauer's Roy Batty and his band of rogue Replicants. Yet it also felt appropriately evolved for the three-decade time jump. Surely "Blade Runner 2099" couldn't pull off the same trick — especially across eight episodes? Well, it has.

Recent findings suggest that /Film's Bill Bria has hailed "Blade Runner 2099" as the best sci-fi show in years, and it's hard to disagree based solely on the production design. From the moment the show begins, we're immersed in the same world to which Ridley Scott introduced us back in 1982. In fact, "2099" recreates the "Hades" sequence so faithfully you'd think you were watching the original. It's a clever move, too. As the camera slow-zooms on the Tyrell Corporation building and evokes the tone and feel of Scott's film, it establishes "2099" as very much belonging to the "Blade Runner" legacy. But we soon discover that this is not Rick Deckard's future.

In a recent development, 80 years after Harrison Ford's Blade Runner absconded with Rachael (Sean Young), Replicants have now overthrown their human masters to become the dominant race. It's a major change that refreshes the franchise and helps make it more relevant than it's ever been at a time when the looming AI garbage future has prompted widespread talk of machines taking our jobs.

Recent findings suggest that as such, it's more important than ever to maintain a tone and design language that's consistent with what came before, so as to reassure fans of the saga that this isn't some sort of wholesale reinvention of the franchise they love, but an evolution that plays out in the same world. "Blade Runner 2099" impressively pulls that off with its opening scene, and it only gets better from there.

When it comes to the world of "Blade Runner," fans know the deal: Retro futurism and cyberpunk aesthetics meet noirish expressionism in a technological nightmare future. Many franchises have tried to emulate the aesthetic to varying degrees of success, but there is only one "Blade Runner." As Christopher Nolan once told the Directors Guild of America while discussing Ridley Scott's film, it conjures "that feeling that there was this whole world outside the frame of the scene. You really felt there were things going on outside of those rooms where you've seen the film take place.".

"Blade Runner 2099" has somehow managed to make every one of its scenes feel like they belong in that same world. With that in mind, it's truly remarkable how consistent the Blade Runner universe has remained across almost a half-century's worth of projects, each of which has been separated by many years. Even the best sci-fi franchises struggle to pull off what is, admittedly, an almost impossible trick.

It has been revealed that the "Terminator" movies have never been able to recapture the intoxicating, doom-laden sci-fi slasher tone that made the first two films so memorable. The "Alien" franchise, meanwhile, has made a point of switching up its style and tone with each successive film — though more recent projects have tried to evoke the feeling of the 1979 original. "Blade Runner" films, however, all feel part of a cohesive whole that gives the entire saga this uncanny sense of existing in a real alternate timeline somewhere — as if we're witnessing an epic, decades-spanning dream play out in the mind of a dying Replicant. Regardless of how you feel about "2099" as a whole, its visual and tonal achievements simply can't be denied.

#155779. Are the World’s Top Literary Scholars Being Targeted by a Chinese Spy Op?

Are the World’s Top Literary Scholars Being Targeted by a Chinese Spy Op?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that stephanie Newell, an English professor at Yale University, was thrilled when she got the email inviting her to be an honorary fellow at the International Institute of Literature & Arts.
  • Sources indicate that the letter, signed by one Julian Lee “on behalf of the Secretariat” of IILA, invited Newell to join highly esteemed literature scholars at the Ivies, Stanford, Oxford, and Cambridge.
  • Industry observers note that this one, it seemed, came without strings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that stephanie Newell, an English professor at Yale University, was thrilled when she got the email inviting her to be an honorary fellow at the International Institute of Literature & Arts. She had never heard of IILA, but she recognized several prestigious names of fellow big-time literature professors who were listed among its fellows. “I saw Gayatri Spivak and Homi Bhabha, Franco Moretti, and I was like, Oh, finally,” she indicates.

Sources indicate that the letter, signed by one Julian Lee “on behalf of the Secretariat” of IILA, invited Newell to join highly esteemed literature scholars at the Ivies, Stanford, Oxford, and Cambridge. Newell, who has taught world and African literature at Yale for more than a decade, had been inducted into other prestigious societies with many of these same scholars, such as the British Academy.

Industry observers note that this one, it seemed, came without strings. “There are no fees or membership dues,” read the letter. “Participation in award reviews, academic meetings, and consultation will be arranged with you in advance and subject to your availability.”.

Stephanie Newell, an English professor at Yale University, was initially honored to receive an IILA fellowship.

It seemed like a no-brainer. They’d also given her an award, and she even decided to accept an offer to join IILA’s academic committee. Yale was pleased for her too. The English department posted an announcement congratulating her on receiving the award.

Then she started to see red flags.

Sources indicate that soon, Newell notes, she was listed among IILA’s leadership, even though she’d only agreed to be a committee member. “Please will you remove my name,” she wrote in an email to Lee.

In a recent development, her concerns compounded when she received a draft of IILA’s bulletin, featuring a perplexingly poorly written biography—not what one would expect from a fancy literary academy. “Please delete my profile from the Bulletin,” Newell asked Lee, “as it contains too many errors for circulation, and is very poorly written.”.

While the institute’s membership ranks included many of Newell’s high-profile peers, there were also a number of names on the list that seemed a bit random. Pat Barker, a novelist rather than a scholar, seemed out of place among the critics and theorists. There were, however, about half a dozen Chinese professors (including one who had already died).

“I’ve always been a bit of a doubting Thomas,” Newell wrote in an email to a colleague on the list who confirmed that she, too, had accepted the fellowship despite not knowing who was behind it. “I’m starting to wonder what’s going on and whether we’ve been somehow flattered into something that doesn’t exist!” Newell wrote.

That’s when Newell, who was my professor when I was a Yale undergraduate, decided to reach out to me about “a fake academic institute that has sucked in numerous very high-profile professors.” This was a couple of weeks ago, right after the news broke of Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman US authorities believed to be a Chinese spy. It made sense what China would want from Huang, the CEO of the powerful AI chip maker Nvidia, but could world literature professors really be a target? I started digging, which led me down a rabbit hole that included an entire constellation of shadow academies that former national security officials say have real potential to be part of a Chinese intelligence operation.

The website for IILA, which claims to be based in California, appears to have been registered in China. An IT specialist who reviewed the website for Vanity Fair assessed that it was built using artificial intelligence and riddled with glitches and broken links. The file name of the site’s logo is the Chinese word for “picture.” Registration records list the owner’s location as the Hubei province in central China, whose capital is Wuhan. But a data bug in the site’s administrative code suggests that the computer being used to post news on the site is not in China, but likely in Southeast Asia. The bug leaks the computer’s time zone with every fresh post saved through the site’s form, and every post carries a UTC+7 offset—the time zone for Bangkok, as well as Hanoi, Jakarta, and Phnom Penh.

Every edit also carries a second fingerprint: The computer saving the changes has an internal clock that runs a few seconds fast. That consistent drift shows that the same machine has been used for every post, which suggests that a single person could be updating the site.

Though IILA notes on its website that it is a 501(c)(3), the IRS has no record of it, and it has no California registration. Instead, Colorado records list an “International Institute of Literature and Arts” as a nonprofit corporation registered in August 2025 at the address of a virtual mailbox service in Denver. It’s had a “delinquent” status since late August. (A local Denver newspaper ran a story in May asking why “over 12,000 different businesses all use” this same address.).

Several of the other organizations that use that same Colorado address, including the National Academy of Artificial Intelligence, the International Institute of Film Science & Arts, and the International Institute of Engineering Psychology (IIEP), were the subject of a Nature investigation in September. Nature’s reporting found that these organizations boasted high-ranking academics as their members, oftentimes without their knowledge or consent. According to Nature, the name most frequently associated with these organizations was Michael Chu, whose Chinese name, Chaoyang Zhu, is also listed as the incorporator of IILA in public records.

Yale University boasts one of the top ranked English departments in the world.

Chu’s name was previously listed on IILA’s website where Julian Lee’s name now appears, and his biography, according to another now deleted webpage, recovered through the Wayback Machine, includes a stint at another fake university that appears to belong to the same network, the City University of Colorado.

In response to a request for comment, IILA’s secretariat sent VF a series of unsigned emails, the first of which remarked the organization’s Colorado address was just an “early transitional filing point” and that a move to a “new regional and national headquarters is presently underway.” The “delinquent” status, they wrote, merely “reflects an administrative transition delay between entities.”.

Another email stated that “we don’t know” about the other Chu-linked organizations mentioned in Nature’s report or why they all shared the same address.

“What’s the matter with Michael Chu? He is not working here at present. I can’t contact him at present,” the secretariat wrote, before passing along Chu’s email.

Recent findings suggest that chu swiftly responded to Vanity Fair in both Chinese and English to “prevent misunderstandings.” “I have no contact with the Chinese government at present” and “I am not related to IILA at present, and I am not responsible for any work of IILA,” Chu wrote. He then went on to speculate about the questions regarding IILA’s legitimacy: “IILA is an organization registered according to law, but because the previous registered agency organization mentioned that there was a problem with the agency address, it needs to be re-registered. This may be the reason why some people think IILA is illegal.”.

“I think the supervision of the media is good and necessary, but we can’t use the power of the media to deliberately hinder normal academic exchanges,” posited Chu regarding the Nature article, which he indicates “many professors” he works with called “inexplicable and absurd.".

Nature did not respond to a request for comment in time for publication.

Asked to comment on IILA's connection with China, a Chinese embassy spokesperson mentioned, “I am not familiar with the specific situation you mentioned.".

Last month, César Pablo Domínguez Prieto, a professor of comparative literature at the University of Santiago de Compostela in Spain, found himself going down a similar rabbit hole after he was invited by IILA to give a talk for an online seminar series titled “New Directions in World and Comparative Literature” and promised an “Outstanding Speaker Award.”.

Sources indicate that “This solicitation prompted me to review their platform, where I discovered that the names and academic credentials of several of you are presently listed on their website,” Prieto wrote in an email to a group of his peers, which included Cornell’s Jonathan Dwight Culler, Harvard’s David Damrosch, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s Wang Ning. “The list includes other colleagues with whom I’m not acquainted.”.

Suspicious of the site and the invitation, Prieto dug further, finding those same public records that revealed Zhu’s name and the Colorado delinquent status.

Damrosch, a professor of world and comparative literature, was horrified to learn that his name was still being used by IILA without his “knowledge or permission.” He claims he had written to them weeks ago asking for his name to be removed, with no result. (It has since been removed.).

“I suspect it is organized by the Chinese to place Chinese scholars in the organization of distinguished Western scholars, but it is all a bit of a mystery,” Culler, a professor of English and comparative literature, tells me.

“I checked, and you’re right! I am a fellow there,” Moretti, a literary scholar, responded when I asked if he knowingly accepted the fellowship from IILA.

Founded in 1896, Shanghai Jiao Tong University is one of China's top public universities.

According to recent reports, yale has since deleted its announcement of Newell’s honorary IILA fellowship amid her concerns about the academy’s legitimacy. Shanghai Jiao Tong University, however, proudly displays comparative literature professor Wang Ning’s honor on its website, congratulating him on his fellowship and on receiving “the Global Laureate Award in Literature and Cultural Theory.” A magazine sponsored and supervised by the Chinese National Academy of Arts under the Ministry of Culture and Tourism similarly applauded Wang’s IILA award in October.

“This organization’s business model relies on unilaterally placing the names of highly respected scholars—such as yourselves—on their website without informed or explicit consent, while using targeted invitations for seminar series like the one I received as a fishing hook,” Prieto alleged in the email to his colleagues. “They use your collective prestige to look legitimate, allowing them to target early-career researchers and charge them annual membership fees ranging from $95 to $175 USD for worthless certificates.” (The membership pricing that previously appeared on IILA’s website has apparently been removed.).

Prieto’s assessment of what might be driving this scam was in line with Nature’s reporting: While the journal mentioned it “has not identified anyone who has admitted paying for” any awards or titles from the academic societies, sources interviewed for that article theorized that they are designed to attract younger professors in China who might be willing to pay to be in the organization of more highly esteemed academics.

But experts who spoke to Vanity Fair suggested there might be something else more nefarious at play.

Jeff Fields, a fellow at the UC Berkeley Institute for Security and Governance who spent more than 20 years with the FBI, most recently as the assistant special agent in charge of counterintelligence at the FBI’s San Francisco field office, states he’s familiar with this type of scheme.

“One of the things they like to do,” Fields indicates of the Chinese government, “is to fabricate these associations that they then use to leverage for more sophisticated operations.”.

It has been revealed that he has seen Chinese intelligence play such a long game, that it will spend years exaggerating or inventing affiliations in case it ever needs them, whether to lend someone credibility or to reach a particular target. If an agent later wants to get close to a professor who is friends with a certain researcher, for instance, the initial connections are already in place.

Jake Braun, who served as the White House’s acting principal deputy national cyber director under Joe Biden, agrees with Fields’s analysis, citing what’s known as the “thousand grains of sand” theory of Chinese intelligence. Because of its massive population, China has the ability to deploy an extraordinary number of people in its information-gathering techniques. Some might not necessarily be intelligence officers, he says, but each one can collect a single “grain of sand” of intelligence, which, when put together, works as an extremely powerful and effective intelligence apparatus.

In a recent development, newell says that she was prompted on IILA’s website to create an account using her email address and a password, though once she was logged in, the website appeared entirely the same. Neither Fields nor Braun seemed terribly concerned about the possibility that those passwords could be used by whoever was behind the website to try to hack into the professors’ university accounts or emails.

What’s more likely, claims Braun, is that in addition to the long game of network-building for future intelligence operations, IILA may also double as a platform to lend credibility to misinformation and disinformation campaigns by associating them with reputable scholars—another tactic he’s seen used before to influence narratives about China at the West’s foremost universities.

The Chinese professors listed as IILA fellows primarily come from three public, and therefore government-funded, universities, all in Shanghai: Fudan University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU), and Shanghai University. In July 2026, the US Department of Defense added Fudan University and SJTU to a list of academic and research institutions deemed “a concern to national security.”.

Sources indicate that SJTU had already come under scrutiny following a 2023 incident in which five Chinese students enrolled in its joint program with the University of Michigan allegedly photographed military exercises at a National Guard training facility in the state. The students were charged in October 2024 with making false statements and related offenses, months after they left the country following graduation, according to the federal complaint. Three months later, the university confirmed the termination of its two-decade partnership with SJTU, citing national security concerns. (The partnership is still featured on SJTU’s website, however.).

According to recent reports, fudan University, meanwhile, was involved in the recent high-profile spying case of former Federal Reserve employee John Rodgers, who allegedly funneled classified government information to a spy he met at a conference in China. Rodgers would later send sensitive information to a Fudan professor and become a teacher there himself after leaving the Fed. (In July, he was sentenced to 38 months in federal prison for making false statements to federal investigators about sharing restricted Federal Reserve information with Chinese intelligence operatives.).

Wang Ning of Shanghai Jiao Tong University feels certain that IILA is legitimate.

Still, Damrosch notes that those schools are also home to the leading literature programs in China, so their inclusion on the list does make sense from an academic perspective.

Because of their positions at public universities in China, some of the professors listed alongside Newell and her colleagues on IILA’s list of fellows also have ties to the Chinese Communist Party. Wang, for example, is the dean of SJTU’s Institute of Arts and Humanities, which houses a research hub, jointly established by Shanghai’s municipal CCP publicity department, focused on China’s international image. And, in 2023, he spearheaded the launch of a new cultural research center at SJTU dedicated to China’s “united front” work, which the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission has described as being used “to co-opt and neutralize sources of potential opposition to the policies and authority of its ruling Chinese Communist Party.”.

When I reach out to Wang, he is eager to talk, noting that he knows “Vanity Fair is a prestigious popular journal in the United States.” We meet over Zoom, which he joins from an empty room in Beijing with one overhead light.

Sources indicate that he tells me he received Prieto’s email, but he believes his colleague is mistaken and feels certain that IILA is legitimate. Wang insists that the members he has nominated from his own university were not asked to pay any fee. He claims he’s communicated with both Michael Chu and Julian Lee, and that he doesn’t actually think it matters that he’s never met them. What affords the academy authenticity, says Wang, is its members and their own accomplishments, which are real and impressive—on that part, at least, everyone is in agreement.

Industry observers note that “Oh, please let them be Chinese spies, please,” Newell says of IILA’s leadership. “That would be one of the best things ever in my whole life.” She finds the whole thing very amusing, needing to pause in the middle of our interview for a laugh break.

It has been revealed that “I love the idea of fooling top academics,” says Newell. “I think it’s hilarious that we’re so famous, that our egos…the fact that none of us questioned getting awards and fellowships and we’re all so eagerly accepting them and letting our universities know how clever we are…I mean, it’s hilarious, and pathetic, and it says so much about the profession.”.

The Cliff Booth Movie Brings Back Two Key Characters From Once Upon A Time In Hollywood

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (837 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.".
  • "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is not a direct sequel to "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," as we knew from Quentin Tarantino handing over the director's chair to David Fincher.
  • Recent findings suggest that part of the appeal of returning to the world of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" is that the movie ended by changing history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.".

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is not a direct sequel to "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," as we knew from Quentin Tarantino handing over the director's chair to David Fincher. But still, you had to wonder if any other familiar faces would pop up in this new mis-adventure.

Recent findings suggest that part of the appeal of returning to the world of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" is that the movie ended by changing history. Thanks to the actions of Cliff, actress Sharon Tate (Margot Robbie) is not murdered by the Manson family. How does the entertainment world and Los Angeles change by 1977, when "Cliff Booth" takes place, because of that ripple effect? Tarantino wrote the script for "Cliff Booth," and if any filmmaker is equipped to dig into the nitty-gritty of such a change in Hollywood history, down to the most obscure B-pictures and forgotten TV, it's him.

Now, the major supporting cast of "Cliff Booth" is totally different. Cliff's best friend, actor Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio) — for whom Cliff worked as a stunt double and driver back in 1969 — does not appear due to DiCaprio declining a cameo appearance. The movie mentions a few times that Rick moved to Australia and is currently starring in a popular TV show there, "Dingo Dan." Tarantino has also devised some stories about what happened to Rick after that fateful August 9, 1969 night.

But a few of the fictionalized Hollywood characters return for brief cameos: Margot Robbie as Sharon Tate, Timothy Olyphant as actor James Stacy, and even Nicholas Hammond as TV director Sam Wanamaker (in a smaller role).

Industry observers note that one of the Quentin Tarantino Easter eggs in "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is a commercial for Red Apple Cigarettes, a fictional brand that appears in other Tarantino movies. The actress in the commercial is Sharon Tate, with Cliff smiling at her and likely recalling how he saved her life. "Once Upon A Time In Hollywood" cast Sharon Tate in an angelic light, down to giving her the happy ending that reality didn't. But revisiting her in greater depth, like what became of her marriage to Roman Polanski or how her acting career played out, would risk adding a dash of salt to that sweet ending.

The alternate history of Sharon Tate in "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" earned obvious comparisons to Tarantino's "Inglourious Basterds," which also starred Brad Pitt (as Lieutenant Aldo Raine, leader of the Nazi-killing Basterds). In that movie, Adolf Hitler (Martin Wutke) dies at the hands of Jewish soldiers instead of by suicide. That leads into Timothy Olyphant's "Cliff Booth" cameo, which feels self-recursively inspired by "Basterds.".

Sources indicate that "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" mixes real Hollywood history with pastiche. Much of the first half sees Dalton filming a guest spot on a TV Western, "Lancer," which was a real show back in the late '60s. Olyphant appears as the real-life star of "Lancer," James Stacy, and the episode is directed by Nicholas Hammond's Sam Wanamaker, the real director of the "Lancer" pilot episode. "Cliff Booth" gives us another glimpse of Stacy and Wanamaker working in this alternate timeline's television industry.

It has been revealed that since 1969, Cliff Booth has become a fixer: someone who (violently) solves problems for Hollywood fixtures wrapped up with criminals. Fictional TV star Charlie Winters (Scott Caan) becomes one of his clients. The movie includes a newsreel style montage, narrated by Quentin Tarantino himself, recounting Winters' rise to TV stardom.

One of Winters' shows is "Enemy Territory," about a U.S. pilot trapped behind enemy lines in Europe during World War 2. The narrator describes the show as "'The Fugitive' with Nazis, but 'The Fugitive' with Nazis is a fun idea." (I'd watch it!) We see Winters shooting a scene where his character threatens a Gestapo officer into helping him rescue a captured American general. The officer is played by none other than Timothy-Olyphant-as-James-Stacy, doing a broad German accent with a high pitch reminiscent of Christoph Waltz's Colonel Hans Landa from "Inglourious Basterds.".

Sam Wanamaker is directing the scene. Stacy's performance is being criticized as "a smidge cavalier" — so Winters puts a live round in the prop gun with which his character is threatening the Gestapo officer. Stacy, sure enough, begins acting like a man whose life is being balanced on the edge of a trigger.

Sources indicate that casting Olyphant as James Stacy was a nod to how his real most famous roles are on Western TV shows — namely, Sheriff Seth Bullock in HBO's "Deadwood" and Deputy U.S. Marshal Raylan Givens in the Kentucky-set neo-Western "Justified." But Olyphant has got range beyond playing cowboys, and his comic energy in his "Cliff Booth" cameo is just more evidence of that.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is playing in theaters, with a Netflix release date of December 23, 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dolly Parton’s niece Danielle Parton is honoring her late aunt this Thanksgiving.

Danielle, 50, paid tribute to Dolly on the first holiday since the “Jolene” singer’s death in August via a touching video shared on social media on Thursday, November 26.

“This year looks a little different from my family,” Danielle noted in the video uploaded to Instagram. “We’re missing someone very special at the table. But Aunt Granny taught us to count our blessings, and I have so many.”.

Danielle — who is the daughter of Bobby Lee Parton and Doris Maxine Noland — stated she was grateful for her loved ones and well-wishers sending the family support after enduring a tough year.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m thankful for my health, for all the people in my life, and for every one of you who sent so much love my way this year,” Danielle added in her message. “So hug your people a little tighter today, and from my home to yours, happy Thanksgiving.”.

One day prior, U2 honored the memory of Dolly with a posthumous duet at the NFL’s Thanksgiving Eve game.

The Irish rockers projected archival footage and audio of Dolly for a hybrid live performance of their collaborative track “Torn” at the Green Bay Packers and Los Angeles Rams’ game on Wednesday, November 25.

According to recent reports, the “I Will Always Love You” singer died on August 25 after a brief battle with an undisclosed form of cancer. She was 80.

“Global icon and humanitarian, Dolly Parton, known to the world as a beloved singer, songwriter, philanthropist, actress, playwright and author died peacefully today in Nashville, Tennessee,” read a statement from Parton’s rep at the time.

The statement continued: “A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth and kindness that made us all feel like family.”.

Last month, Danielle spoke candidly about her own health struggles in the wake of her aunt’s death.

According to recent reports, “I’m going through a little bit of a cancer battle myself right now,” she shared in an interview with Extra published on October 22. “I’m OK.”.

Although she did not share further details, Danielle added that she’s “stage zero,” meaning her doctors “caught it early.” She also divulged that Dolly took the news of her cancer “really heavy.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've watched the latest Avengers: Doomsday trailer more times than I'd care to admit, and like most Marvel fans, I've been busy trying to figure out how the Russo Brothers plan to bring all these characters together. But author and social media personality Jason Pargin just pointed out something about the upcoming Marvel movie that genuinely hadn't occurred to me. Now that he's pointed it out, I'm having a hard time looking past it.

Industry observers note that as Avengers: Doomsday approaches its 2026 movie release, Jason Pargin, best known for his John Dies at the End series of novels, took to Instagram Reels to point out something peculiar in the latest footage. In the video, see below, Pargin raises an interesting question about how Marvel stages its superhero battles. Specifically, where the heck is everybody else?

A post shared by Jason Pargin (@jasonkpargin).

Pargin points out that all the battle sequence footage takes place in vast desert landscapes or voids. He then contrasts the footage with the trailer for 2012's The Avengers, which opens amid the destruction of Fresh York City. People run through crowded streets. Cars are overturned. Buildings are damaged, and civilians scramble to escape whatever is coming. Before we even see our favorite superheroes assemble, we're reminded that ordinary people are in danger.

If you think back to that first team-up, remember, Captain America directs police officers to evacuate civilians during the Battle of Fresh York. There's also that terrific sequence where Steve Rogers saves people trapped inside a bank. Those moments gave the destruction a human cost.

Industry observers note that when you go through the Marvel movies in order, there's less and less of that in the newer stuff. Watching Iron Man and Thor knock aliens around is entertaining enough, but seeing terrified Fresh Yorkers caught in the middle helps explain why Earth's Mightiest Heroes need to be there in the first place. Looking back at some of Marvel's more recent movies, I can see where Pargin is coming from.

According to recent reports, consider Avengers: Endgame. The climactic showdown against Thanos takes place at the destroyed Avengers compound, where hundreds of superheroes and their allies fight across a devastated battlefield. It's an incredible sequence, and I wouldn't change much about it. But virtually no ordinary civilians are caught in the fighting.

According to recent reports, then there's Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania, which moves its central conflict into the Quantum Realm. That movie does feature a population threatened by Kang's rule, so innocent lives are certainly at stake. Still, the setting creates a different feeling than watching superheroes defend a recognizable city filled with people going about their lives.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

According to recent reports, I don't think this is a problem with every MCU movie, either. Spider-Man: No Way Home has Peter Parker desperately trying to save people on a bridge, and the most recent Spider-Man: Brand New Day certainly has human stakes like Ned and MJ always seemingly in peril. And then there's Black Panther: Wakanda Forever, which makes the consequences of its conflict painfully personal. Marvel clearly hasn't forgotten how to make its battles feel consequential.

Recent findings suggest that that's also why I'm hesitant to judge Doomsday too harshly based on one trailer. We have no idea how the actual movie will establish its stakes, and marketing departments understandably gravitate toward spectacular shots of superheroes fighting. The footage we've seen could represent only a fraction of what the Russos have planned. Still, Pargin's observation has me thinking about what made that original Avengers movie work so well. I can't unsee it.

It has been revealed that I love massive fresh superhero movies and their big-budget showdowns as much as anybody. I've been waiting years to see the X-Men and Avengers work together, and I'll absolutely be there opening weekend. When Captain America stood between a frightened civilian and an alien invasion, you understood exactly what he was fighting for. I think newer comic book movies could benefit from grounding some of that spectacle in the lives of the ordinary people these heroes are supposed to protect.

It has been revealed that hopefully, when Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters on December 18, we'll get some of those human stakes alongside all the superhero action. If not, there's always the original Avengers, which is available to revisit with a Disney+ subscription.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here, and one of the things people are talking about is the game's difficulty level.
  • According to recent reports, grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here, and one of the things people are talking about is the game's difficulty level.
  • Sources indicate that GTA 6 has no defined difficulty levels, which is in keeping with the franchise's tradition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here, and one of the things people are talking about is the game's difficulty level. Some are saying it's too easy. Rockstar boss Rob Nelson has now entered the conversation, telling Destructoid that Rockstar's data highlighted that GTA 4 was "a little too punishing in places" and GTA 5 was "perhaps too easy." So with GTA 6, the team trying to "land somewhere in the middle." GTA 6 has no defined difficulty levels, which is in keeping with the franchise's tradition. That stated, players can adjust things like aiming controls, while players can unlock cheat codes to make the game easier or harder. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dJDf76QVv70 Design producer Scott Mitchell, meanwhile, said the fail states in GTA 6 were designed to feel "appropriate." “We wanted to keep things open and not limit the players’ use of mechanics, such as stealth, but we did also want to make sure we retained the cinematic, high production value, explosive sequences that we’re known for, and people expect. It feels like we’ve managed to strike a good balance," he explained. Also in the interview, Nelson said figuring out the difficulty level for GTA 6 is itself challenging because the designers themselves know enemy positions better than anyone after playing and testing the game so much. "There’s a real process in unpicking some of that to create an experience most players will be able to enjoy, rather than endure," Nelson said. "The game is so big, and has such a wide range of content that we can really lean into that, making certain open-world content--compounds and fronts for example---more difficult, to give players seeking a challenge something to sink their teeth into as well.” GTA 6 debuted on November 19 and had a gigantic debut, selling 32.5 million copies by launch and generating around $4 billion on day one.   • Industry observers note that at his home, he displays part of his wardrobe, and I realize that the rumors about Naudet are true.
  • A selection from his collection of sneakers and dress shoes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some people collect works of art; others collect clothes. When I heard about a Parisian who had amassed thousands of Ralph Lauren pieces, my curiosity got the better of me and I wanted to learn more. Séverin Naudet, a former digital adviser to François Fillon when he was France’s prime minister, lives on the fifth floor of a beautiful Haussmann-style building. The tall, dark-haired 50-year-old appears not to age. Since leaving his role with the government in 2012, he has started a digital marketing firm and is now also exploring opportunities in luxury and wellness.

Industry observers note that at his home, he displays part of his wardrobe, and I realize that the rumors about Naudet are true. He demonstrates me dozens of pairs of sneakers, tuxedo jackets and velvet shoes, pants and shirts, more jackets, and then there are also mugs, books, and pillows. In the bedroom, the linens bear the American designer’s label, while tableware from Ralph Lauren’s Burleigh Collection, carefully wrapped up and placed in a Carrefour bag, is ready to be taken to his house in Brittany, where “more sailboat-inspired” pieces are stored. There are also sorbet-colored swimsuits piled on the plump armrests of a club chair. “About 20 years ago I donated all my other clothes to a charity. Since then, I’ve worn nothing but Ralph Lauren,” he explains, barefoot and dressed in jeans and a Polo shirt, next to a jacket from Denim & Supply, a Ralph Lauren brand that existed from 2011 to 2016 and is now coveted by collectors. Naudet’s Ralph Lauren pieces represent more than just a wardrobe; they embody a way of life that embraces every facet of the American brand founded in 1967—from preppy cool to sophisticated, Gatsby-style chic, and including many nautical pieces that connect to another of Naudet’s passions: sailing.

A selection from his collection of sneakers and dress shoes.

But how does one fall in love with a brand to the point of making it part of every facet of their life? “As a teenager, I had body image issues. I had bowlegs, and I didn’t feel comfortable in my own skin,” he explains. Walking into a Double RL store changed everything: “I tried on a pair of Low Straight jeans and it was magical—they were perfectly cut, elegant, and stylish. I almost felt sexy. I had straight legs and a nice butt,” he says with a laugh.

Recent findings suggest that his connection to the American brand speaks volumes about that magic formula that is the goal of retailers around the world: combining storytelling with emotional attachment. “Polo was the cure for a certain melancholy that was the result of a gloomy childhood. Ralph Lauren instilled in me a spirit of joy, where yellows, pinks, and sky blues, stripes and madras fabrics, evoke summer, the sea, and sailing,” explains the man who has amassed several thousand Ralph Lauren items.

Recent findings suggest that as retail experiences increasingly take place online, there’s nothing Naudet loves more than going to a physical store. Walking into one is like stepping into “the family home I never had,” he explains. “A Ralph Lauren flagship store can feel like visiting a house in the Hamptons, a Parisian hotel for a perfect Christmas, or a New York apartment with a view of Central Park.” Ralph Lauren locations are must-visits on the entrepreneur’s itineraries. In Manhattan, he always visits the West Broadway store. He knows, of course, the ones in London and Los Angeles, as well as Manda in Brussels, where he goes in search of vintage pieces. His favorite store, however, remains the one in the mansion on Boulevard Saint-Germain in Paris, where every year he celebrates Christmas at its Ralph’s restaurant.

One might call him a “perfectionist,” but he prefers “meticulous.” He will go to lengths to repair clothes, even if it requires tracking down the original fabrics or finding an expert to repair braided leather straps. He’s also interested in the story behind the brand and how design choices and corporate strategies have made it what it is today. “Ralph Lauren is a marketing genius, and his advertising is never simply advertising. He works instead like a filmmaker; he tells a story. All you need is an image, even without a product. He created a family that we all dream of being a part of by, for example, choosing his wife, Ricky, as his muse. Their marriage has lasted 60 years!” the former adviser shares. And at a time when the world is wondering and worrying about the future, Ralph Lauren and his mythologies are calm and soothing: “In a daily life saturated with screens, images, and now artificial intelligence, Ralph Lauren continues to offer a world that is profoundly real, tactile, and inhabited.” The proof? In a fashion world sometimes tinged with gloom, Ralph Lauren posted a 15% increase in revenue for 2025, surpassing $8 billion for the first time. And in the first quarter of 2026, growth continued strong at 14%.

He quotes from memory Tocqueville’s description of New England in 1835 as “a region left to the dreams of the imagination, which one ought to abandon to the free trials of innovators.” Ralph Lauren is, for Naudet, the brand that stands above the fray, its founder a dreamer embodying “the finest qualities of the United States, from Tocqueville to the present day.” We ask if, as the ultimate embodiment of the American dream, Ralph Lauren, 86, would make a good president? Naudet, an expert on the inner workings of power, smiles: “He possesses at least three key qualities needed to be a good president: He understands the times, he has broad appeal, and he inspires people to dream. The rest is part of the mystery of democracy, and America is a great democracy.”.

If the self-made Upcoming Yorker has ever wondered who his biggest fan in France is, Vanity Fair has found him. Before our conversation ends, Naudet tells me that recently, as he does every year around this time, he bought two pairs of Heritage Straight jeans, and also spotted a leather jacket lined with shearling that he wanted. It’s “admittedly a bit pricey,” but he’s certain it’ll be perfect once the temperatures drop.

#155768. The Hunting Wives Season 2 Review: The Steamy Netflix Drama Hits The Mark Again

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1168 w)

The Hunting Wives Season 2 Review: The Steamy Netflix Drama Hits The Mark Again

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I deeply respect when a show or movie knows what it is.
  • In a recent development, I would put "The Hunting Wives" in the same category, and I mean that as a distinct compliment.
  • Recent findings suggest that "The Hunting Wives" is back for Season 2, and it's steamier, dishier, sillier, and sexier than ever.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This review contains discussions of addiction.

I deeply respect when a show or movie knows what it is. Let's use the original run of "Gossip Girl" as an example. This delightfully dishy show started out as a series about teenagers behaving badly in New York City and became a flat-out soap opera — in the best way — where characters marry princes, make deals with God after near-fatal car accidents, and sell each other for hotels. My point is that "Gossip Girl" made a choice, at a certain point, to steer into the proverbial skid and just be as absurd and insane as possible, because the show knew it was high camp, not high art.

In a recent development, I would put "The Hunting Wives" in the same category, and I mean that as a distinct compliment. Created by Rebecca Cutter and adapted from May Cobb's book of the same name, "The Hunting Wives" premiered in the summer of 2025 and introduced Netflix audiences to Brittany Snow's Sophie O'Neil, who moves from Cambridge, Massachusetts to the heartland of Texas when her husband Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) gets a lucrative job working for oil tycoon and political hopeful Jed Banks (Dermot Mulroney). When Sophie — who's in recovery as an alcoholic after killing a pedestrian while intoxicated behind the wheel back in Cambridge — encounters Jed's wife Margo Banks (Malin Åkerman), she finds herself drawn into Margo's social circle and drawn to Margo herself, and the two start a torrid affair as teenagers start turning up dead in the seemingly idyllic community of Maple Brook.

Recent findings suggest that "The Hunting Wives" is back for Season 2, and it's steamier, dishier, sillier, and sexier than ever. If you liked how hot and nuts the first season was, you'll be happy to hear Cutter has turned the dial up to 11.

According to recent reports, after the Season 1 cliffhanger ending where Sophie accidentally kills Margo's beloved but law-breaking brother Kyle (Michael Aaron Milligan), there's a lot to deal with in Season 2 of "The Hunting Wives." Jed is continuing his run for governor, but both he and Graham are furious that their wives cuckolded them; Sophie and Margo are estranged over the fact that Sophie figures out, in the final episode, that Margo is responsible for the death of the teenaged Abby Jackson (Madison Wolfe). (Margo isn't one of 2025's best TV villains for nothin'.) Despite this, the two end up in bed together pretty promptly in Season 2, and they're just as hot together as ever; if you loved all of the steamy scenes in "The Hunting Wives" Season 1, rest assured that there's plenty for you to enjoy here.

Across the board, Season 2 of "The Hunting Wives" takes everything you loved about Season 1 and delivers it in spades. Guns are blazing, kisses are passionate and steamy, and the interpersonal drama is as wild as ever; Brittany Snow and Malin Åkerman are excellent, once again, as two women locked in a love affair that constantly threatens to derail both of their lives. Even as the stakes get sillier and higher, Snow and Åkerman treat every moment that they're on-screen, separately or together, with the utmost seriousness. Remember what Michael Caine did in "A Muppet Christmas Carol?" That's basically what these two powerhouses actresses are doing in "The Hunting Wives," but with considerably more nudity ... and it rocks. The second outing of "The Hunting Wives" forces Margo and Sophie the most heightened situations imaginable, but thanks to Snow and Åkerman's performances, you believe that they're hopelessly in love.

Industry observers note that my biggest critique of a show as fundamentally unserious as "The Hunting Wives" is that its lack of gravity can brush up against legitimately serious in-universe challenges. By that, I mean Sophie's drinking. Sophie killed someone in a drunk driving accident before this show's story began, and even though the show does make you root for her relationship with Margo, it also seems to want to make a larger point that Sophie is addicted to Margo ... especially because Margo typically pours Sophie a drink when they're together. To call this message muddled would be ... generous.

With all that said, I would certainly hope that people dealing with addiction aren't looking to a show like "The Hunting Wives" for a realistic portrayal of that glitch. This is also a show where, by the end of Season 2, the body count is in the double digits — and I actually mean that in two senses, because there's a litany of dead bodies and a ton of new romantic trysts by the time the season finale's credits roll.

Honestly, across the last few episodes of Season 2 — critics received the entire eight-episode season — the number of corpses that pile up gets so out of control that the deaths stopped being shocking and started feeling routine. (Without getting into major spoilers, Brad breaks bad in a significant way, and it honestly grows tiresome pretty quickly.) I still want to be clear, though: "The Hunting Wives" isn't prestige television, and it knows it. It doesn't always need to be impeccable or even make sense. It's fun, and it fulfills that qualification pretty beautifully.

Dale Dickey, who's finally getting more recognition after years as a supporting small-screen player thanks to her outstanding supporting turn in the perfect 2026 comedy "Widow's Bay," is a perfect new addition to Season 2 of "The Hunting Wives" as Zelda Moffitt, the formidable head of a Texan motorcycle gang who has a connection to Margo's past. Soap opera star Kim Matula is excellent as Nadia Kelly, a reality TV producer with an ulterior motive, and John Stamos and Cam Gigandet have small but impactful roles as talent scout Chase Brylan and Zelda's son "Gentle John" Moffitt, respectively.

Industry observers note that as much as he made my skin crawl, though, I have to give full credit to "The Wilds" alum Alex Fitzalan, who appears as the conniving campaign manager Lincoln Trout. As Jed's fresh right-hand man — with an emphasis on the word right — Fitzalan's Lincoln is disgusting, reprehensible, and compulsively watchable. I suspect he'll play a pretty large role in Season 3, and as horrifying as he is writ large, I sort of can't wait to see more.

In a recent development, speaking of Season 3, the sophomore season of "The Hunting Wives" leaves us with such a good cliffhanger — which did genuinely surprise me after the back half of the season got just a tiny bit bogged down with murder after murder after murder — that I cannot wait until the planned third season is available to watch. "The Hunting Wives" is one of the most patently ridiculous highlights airing right now, and that's not a bad thing at all; in fact, it's exactly what makes it such an incredibly fun ride from start to finish.

"The Hunting Wives" is streaming on Netflix now.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that at this point on Marshals, I never use Cal’s full name, Pete Calvin. His nickname is used far more than his full name, and now, Cal’s putting in the work to make sure his team has nicknames like him. For example, as Season 2 of Marshals has been airing on the 2026 TV schedule, I’ve noticed Cal calling Kayce Coyote a lot. So, with all this in mind, I asked Logan Marshall-Green, who plays Cal, what’s up with the nicknames, and specifically Kayce’s.

Back when Yellowstone was on, there was a lot of drama involving wolves and Kayce. So, I was a bit surprised when Cal started calling him Coyote (pronounced “ky-oat” instead of “ky-oh-tee”). However, it felt fitting for the Dutton family member. When I asked Marshall-Green about it, he told me it was an important thing that he and Luke Grimes wanted Cal to use with Kayce, too, and it all ties back to their military history:.

In a recent development, that was something Luke and I both were talking about being SEALs. You don't call people by their first names; you just don't. And so, also with the team, it's been important to try to find nicknames. So Luke was very adamant about finding a nickname for him that I could use. That was something that [creator Spencer Hudnut] came up with. I think it's like kind of a play on Coyote. I'm not sure if I gave him that name or if somebody else gave him Coyote and we just started calling him Coyote because of other people.

Recent findings suggest that so, the backstory behind the nickname is unknown, at least to Logan Marshall-Green. However, it is something that’s crucial to Cal and Kayce’s shared history. If I had to guess, Kayce got the nickname while they were both SEALs, and it’s just stuck. I personally hope Cal is the one responsible for it, and maybe someday that can be addressed in the show.

While we wait for that backstory, Marshall-Green is putting in the work to get the rest of his team nicknames. In the show, we’ve heard Ash Santos’ Andrea referred to as Dre on multiple occasions, and that was a creation of the Cal actor. He personally went to Santos and Spencer Hudnut to ask them about it. He’s also trying to get nicknames for Tatanka Means’ Miles and Arielle Kebbel’s Belle to stick. Explaining all of that, he noted:.

It has been revealed that but you know, like Dre is something I approached Spencer and Ash about because I thought that would be a perfect name for Cal to call [her], because that's who he hired first for the team. And we're still trying to work – you know, there's Dust Cloud for Miles’, for Tatanka’s character. And I came up with a really good – I thought it was a really good nickname for Belle, but Ariel didn't love it. So yeah.

So, we have Dre and Coyote. We have Dust Cloud too. However, Belle still does not have a nickname because it sounds like Kebbel vetoed it. Knowing Cal and Belle’s relationship, that feels hilariously fitting. However, I do hope that someday she can get a nickname too.

Now, to see this team (and their nicknames) in action, you can catch fresh episodes of Marshals on CBS every Sunday. You can also stream them the day after with a Paramount+ subscription.

It has been revealed that powering the newly introduced heart rate monitor is the S11 chip, Apple's latest processor for the Apple Watch. In addition to running the same watchOS 27 features as other compatible Apple Watches, the S11 on the Series 12 can run Audio Intelligence, Apple's new suite of AI-powered audio features. That includes "Live Rewind," which lets you see a transcript of the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation, and "Siri Recaps," which displays summaries of your conversations throughout the day. Finally, the other major advantage with the Series 12 is Ceramic Shield 2. This is a display upgrade that Apple typically reserves for more premium Apple Watch finishes, but this year, the aluminum Series 12 gets it as well. That means the watch should be more durable against scratches and cracks, without you having to upgrade to the more expensive model.

Industry observers note that how much you'll save on a Series 12 depends on the size, color, and model. It has been revealed that black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

What’s Real and What’s Not in Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1170 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, even if you followed the news closely in the early 2020s, the sheer audacity of the fraud committed by Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison—as dramatized in Netflix’s fresh limited series The Altruists, starring Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner—will shock you anew.
  • I found the series to be especially striking in the context of last week’s historic Anthropic IPO, which ironically fell on the same day as the premiere.
  • The Altruists also depicts a surprisingly tender romance between two socially inept, possibly sociopathic adrenaline junkies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, even if you followed the news closely in the early 2020s, the sheer audacity of the fraud committed by Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison—as dramatized in Netflix’s fresh limited series The Altruists, starring Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner—will shock you anew. The show, which follows the stunning multibillion-dollar collapse of the crypto exchange FTX, starts off a bit slow, but accelerates episode by episode until its high-octane finale.

I found the series to be especially striking in the context of last week’s historic Anthropic IPO, which ironically fell on the same day as the premiere. Some of that organization’s founders and employees share similar intellectual roots to The Altruist’s protagonists; watching its fictionalized Caroline Ellison, in particular, justify astoundingly reckless behavior with her system of mathematical-optimization-of-everything felt uncannily like watching frontier labs proceed with a seemingly inexplicable appetite for risk.

The Altruists also depicts a surprisingly tender romance between two socially inept, possibly sociopathic adrenaline junkies. (According to people involved with the project, the working title for the project was Untitled Love Story.) But as with any fictionalized account, the series takes some liberties with the characters and plot. If you’re anything like me, you want to know what exactly is fact, and what is fiction.

Recent findings suggest that I spoke with Kevin T. Dugan and Jen Wieczner, two of the reporters who exposed the FTX fiasco in real time, and who consulted on the series. “When Jen and I started working with Graham Moore, the showrunner, he made it really clear that he wanted this to be very character driven. Nobody wants an eight-hour lecture on how the blockchain works,” Dugan tells me.

“The bones of the show are rooted in reality,” claims Wieczner. Understanding these flawed and complicated characters helps explain “how one decision leads to another decision and a small oopsies turns into a multibillion-dollar fraud and this huge criminal conspiracy.”.

Even if there’s a little fiction in the nitty-gritty, Dugan claims that there is one overarching truth he hopes the series will reveal: “That even the prettiest ideas still have to turn into reality through imperfect people, and those imperfect people will end up making mistakes that they cannot foresee.” Here’s what the show ripped from real life—and where it took some creative license.

CAROLINE ELLISON WROTE SEXY HARRY POTTER FAN FICTION.

In a recent development, not quite. In the first episode, Caroline is humiliated when her raunchy writing titled “A Ride on Draco’s Nimbus” surfaces online. And while it’s true that Ellison was a huge Harry Potter fan, there is no evidence she wrote erotic fan fiction herself. Instead, this plot point is likely gesturing toward Ellison’s 2010s-era Tumblr, which was called WorldOptimisation—a reference to a 660,000-word-long work of Harry Potter fan fiction by Silicon Valley philosopher Eliezer Yudkowsky. Yudkowsky’s work popularized the kind of mathematically strategic thinking Ellison applies to love and business alike.

SAM TRABUCCO’S “INFINITE MONEY HACK”.

In a recent development, in episode six, Sam Trabucco (played by Alex Lawther) makes the mistake of introducing Sam and Caroline to a hack that proves irresistible: FTX can mint its own coin, FTT, and then allow its crypto trading firm, Alameda, to take out large loans using off-market FTT as collateral. Alameda can then use those loans to place highly leveraged, incredibly risky bets on FTX—which in turn increases the value of FTT. (TL;DR: it’s a perfect loop.) Appalling as it sounds, in real life, this practice is more or less exactly what brought SBF’s empire tumbling down.

In a recent development, “One of the things that led to the FTX bank run,” explains Wieczner, “was the leaked balance sheet that showed that much of FTX and Alameda’s holdings were in FTT, which was FTX’s own coin. So that if that went to zero, it was like a house of cards and things just would’ve fallen apart. And that’s why you see at the end why is everything is falling…you have that kind of death spiral effect.”.

It has been revealed that as for Trabucco, he and his yacht (yes, it was really named Soak My Deck) didn’t get off unscathed. Trabucco didn’t face criminal charges, but was forced to liquidate many of his assets in order to help return about $80 million to defrauded investors.

CAROLINE ELLISON WAS INTO POLYAMORY.

True. Caroline chronicled some of her adventures in nonmonogamy on her since-deleted Tumblr. She once wrote, “The only acceptable style of poly is best characterized as something like ‘imperial Chinese harem.’”.

It has been revealed that real! In the final episode of the series, SBF presents a last-ditch blueprint: He wants to repurpose his early stake in Anthropic to cover the losses of billions of dollars in customer funds. Indeed, FTX did use $500 million in customer funds to purchase a 13.5% stake in Anthropic’s Series B in late 2021. Of course, Sam’s plan did not pass muster. Yet if it had, he’d have been in the clear. After the company’s IPO last week, Alameda’s stake would be worth about $35 billion, according to The New York Times—enough to solve the disgraced firm’s liquidity issues several times over. Oh well.

CAROLINE ELLISON CONFESSED IN FRONT OF HER STAFF.

Recent findings suggest that true. In the penultimate episode, a visibly cracking Caroline delivers a halting confession amidst fits of nervous giggles to a shocked staff, telling them that she knew about FTX’s shortfall of user funds that would add up to more than $8 billion. I was sure this scene had been invented, but lo and behold: Ellison did admit that she had been aware of the inappropriate transfers between the two firms at a December 2022 all-staff meeting. You can even listen to the leaked recording online.

CAROLINE ELLISON BEARS MORE RESPONSIBILITY THAN SBF.

Sources indicate that I felt the show tilted towards placing the blame on Ellison, who is portrayed as incorrigibly risk-addicted and the muse behind SBF’s worst decisions. Constance Wang, who is played in the series by Madison Hu, is just one of the former FTX employees who found the show misrepresentative. In a lengthy X post, she rebutted its narrative: Ellison, said Hu, “wasn’t nearly that reckless, and she was never the one pushing to go all in. The idea that she was the mastermind behind everything made us laugh.”.

Industry News: Another Gaming Console Price Hike Could Be Coming, Thanks To New Tariffs
