It has been revealed that one of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone. Even if you’re the only person in the auditorium, somebody thought about what you might like to watch, put it on the calendar, and made sure there was a place for you to sit.

That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.

Earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night. Continuing that exercise over Thanksgiving weekend reveals another delightful cross-section of American film culture — albeit with considerably more cannibalism. Related Stories ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation.

At the Music Box Theatre in Chicago, where audiences have spent more than two decades celebrating Thanksgiving by singing along to “The Sound of Music,” moviegoers can also catch Ruggero Deodato’s “Cannibal Holocaust” late Friday night. It’s hard to imagine the Von Trapps sticking around for that one, but there’s something lovely about a neighborhood institution accommodating both crowds.

It has been revealed that in Seattle, the Beacon is observing its own Thanksgiving tradition with “Blood Rage,” the gloriously ridiculous slasher that made cranberry sauce an enduring point of reference for a certain subset of horror fans. For a somewhat more realistic depiction of the horrors of going home for Thanksgiving, SALA Event Center in Los Alamos, New Mexico, is showing Jodie Foster’s “Home for the Holidays.”.

Recent findings suggest that in Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Brattle Theatre is celebrating Black Friday with a double feature of “Chopping Mall” and “Night of the Comet.” If you’d rather watch people die in a shopping mall than go to one yourself, that’s certainly an economical alternative. Meanwhile, Minneapolis’ Trylon Cinema is spending the biggest shopping weekend of the year celebrating the work of documentary filmmaker Barbara Kopple, screening her Oscar-winning “Harlan County, U.S.A.” and “American Dream” as part of a series dedicated to class struggle.

Thanksgiving also marks the 50th anniversary of the Band’s legendary farewell concert, held at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom in 1976. At Film Streams in Omaha, Nebraska, audiences can spend Friday morning watching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz.” That half a century later, people are still getting together to experience a concert most of them weren’t alive to attend speaks to one of the more miraculous things movies can do.

Industry observers note that and in Portland, Oregon, stop-motion animation studio LAIKA is expressing its gratitude to its hometown audience by offering free screenings of “Wildwood“ on Sunday at theaters across the area, including the historic Hollywood Theatre. Considering how many thousands of hours of human labor go into making a stop-motion animated feature, there’s something especially sweet about giving people whose real home served as the setting a chance to enjoy the outcome together.

Of course, what Americans celebrate on Thanksgiving — and whether they celebrate it at all — varies considerably. On Wednesday, California Indian Nations College is presenting a free screening of “People of the West,” a documentary series examining the history of California’s Indigenous peoples from Indigenous perspectives, in Palm Desert. At the historic Raymond Theatre in Raymond, Washington, a free Saturday screening of a documentary about the Qwayat Canoe Society’s journey to Nisqually offers an opportunity to learn more about a living Indigenous tradition.

It has been revealed that and for anyone navigating a particularly painful holiday season, a film festival in Magnolia, Texas, is making a different kind of space. Presented by the nonprofit My Grief Angels, Grief Fest is hosting an in-person community screening on Black Friday, with films also available to watch virtually throughout Thanksgiving weekend. Dedicated to exploring loss and healing through cinema, the festival recognizes just how complicated an invitation to celebrate can be.

In a recent development, there are innumerable ways to spend a long weekend like this, and movies aren’t a substitute for the people we wish we could spend it with. But the wonderful thing about indie exhibition is just how much of it depends on random people thinking about other random people. Someone has to remember that a certain movie exists. Then someone else has to think it might mean something to you. And finally a different person has to care enough to bring it all together.

Whether you’re somebody who spends every Thanksgiving with the same people or a cinephile whose traditions are still taking shape, consider making a little time for your local movie theater this weekend. Thank the person who takes your ticket, and tell the programmer when you love something they booked. Maybe even invite that friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with.

There are so many extraordinary works of art to see in this lifetime and never quite enough time to see them all. How lucky we are to get to watch some of them together.

Recent findings suggest that team Cherry released Hollow Knight: Silksong on Sept. 4, 2025, and the response was passionate, to say the least. Originally revealed in February 2019, six-plus years of anticipation created a fandom-fueled hype cycle that erupted when the game finally got a concrete release date just two weeks before its launch. Other studios scrambled to avoid Silksong’s impact radius, delaying their September-bound games by weeks or months to avoid direct competition. When Silksong's release date arrived, so many players rushed to nab it that digital storefronts like Steam and the Nintendo eShop buckled under the immense server load, leading to a few more hours of Silksong deprivation. By December of last year, the game had already sold a staggering 7 million copies, putting it nearly halfway to the similarly impressive 15 million in sales that its predecessor slowly accrued over several years.

Industry observers note that while Silksong was generally praised by critics and players alike, its skull-crushing difficulty proved a point of contention. From gatekeepers like the hulking Judge to a hidden late-game boss gauntlet that ratcheted up the torment even further, it was relentless. But many of those who came out on the other side (potentially with at least one controller-shaped hole in a wall) looked back on the game’s sharp controls, evocative world, and trying encounters with a Stockholm Syndrome-style sentimentality.

We’ll find out whether Sea of Sorrow takes the game’s difficulty to even greater sicko extremes when it’s released Dec. 11 for Linux, Mac, Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X.

Recent findings suggest that the coming-of-age drama set in Watts, California sees the actress play a mother named Lozita doing her best to hold her family together while there’s inscrutable tension between her partner, recently released from prison, and their imaginative 12-year-old son. “I started out in theater, so to me, it’s never been about a paycheck,” joked Brooks. “It’s always been about the story and what you’re putting out into the world. And so, when I watched [Thompson-Hernandez’s] short, I was like, ‘Yo, this is different. I ain’t never seen nothing like this.’ And it was captivating just the way he was shooting it.”.

Expanding on what drew her to the project, which came to her during her time bouncing between Los Angeles awards press for “The Color Purple,” and the Fresh Zealand set of “A Minecraft Movie,” Brooks said “They handed me the script and it was really the conversation, sitting down with Walter, his passion for his community, hearing about the real Lozita who had unfortunately passed away from cancer two years prior, hearing about the Compton Cowboys, just getting to talk to him about relationships between kids and their parents and the complications that it can bring.”.

She mentioned, “I like the balance. I got to have a little comedy, but I got to do some drama and it does my heart well.” While “Minecraft” brought her “laughs all day with Jack Black and Jason Momoa,” “If I Go” brought Brooks “purpose.” “I’m excited that we get to share stories like this where people are really dealing with their personal concerns and healing and all of that stuff,” she said.

According to recent reports, having screened the film in Los Angeles the night before, Brooks said “You can feel the energy of everyone feeling super represented and feeling a sense of ownership. It’s cool hearing the audience be like, ‘Yeah, yeah,’ When you talk about the planes passing by, or the story about the fuel engines falling on elementary schools. People remember and know that to be a part of what has happened in LA, and the fabric of LA.”.

Sources indicate that one job that was foundational to how she approaches projects like “If I Go” happens to be Brooks’ breakout role as Taystee on “Orange Is the Upcoming Black.” Coming out of the prestigious Julliard School, her mind was more so on “how am I going to make my money for the subway and pay for my college tuition and how am I going to pay for this PB&J sandwich?,” when she booked the role on the series for the then-nascent streaming service Netflix. “I didn’t know what I was stepping into at the time. ‘Orange’ was looked at as a webseries, so nobody knew what this was about to be. But once we got into the work, I was like, ‘Oh, this is deeper than that.’ I remember talking to people who’ve been incarcerated, and I remember even doing a clothing drive for women who have just come out of prison so that they could have clothes for job interviews and stuff like that. We were really invested in the community and giving back,” remarked Brooks.

It has been revealed that “We had that as a group, as storytellers, but then individually, I was watching my co-stars have a point of view, have something to say. And so, I [was] just learning that being an artist is also a form of activism,” she stated. “That was one of the beginning seeds planted in my head once I was in the industry, because I’ve always known that what we do is about service, that’s number one. But I hadn’t experienced that on this level.”.

Since then, Brooks’ goal has been to tell at least one story a year that incorporates a bit of activism, and with “If I Go,” the actress and producer has been more active than ever. “I’ve deemed us the little engine that could, because I really believe that we can take this far. My goal is that we just get as many eyeballs on it as we can. But the truth of the matter is nothing moves like money does. And that’s what I’ve learned is you’ve got to get really creative and strategic about how you can push a movie into the face of the people when you don’t have the money.”.

According to recent reports, “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” distributed by Rich Spirit, has truly been an indie success story, making over $1 million at the box office from the humblest of beginnings. As Brooks noted, that haul has been hard fought, with her, Thompson-Hernandez, and her co-star J. Alphonse Nicholson touring as much of the country as they can to screen the film, and even abroad. “I’m going to Africa this week, I got invited, but then I learned there’s a film festival in Africa. So, I’m like, ‘Can we take the film to Africa?’ And they said, ‘Yes.’ So now, the film’s going to be in the festival there,” said the actress.

Industry observers note that she continued, “It’s even in the form of fashion. People pay attention to what you’re wearing and then they’re like, ‘Why you got that on? Oh! She had a premiere.’ Boom. It’s insane how many tricks I have been working to get people to pay attention to this film that is worth paying attention to.”.

Industry observers note that one of the more beautiful aspects of this “If I Go” experience has been the way in which her community has shown up for her and the film. Snoop Dogg and Ava DuVernay have Instagrammed about it, while Helen Hunt and André Holland have even hosted talk backs for the film. But in terms of creativity, one marketing strategy takes the cake. “Issa Rae, even at her restaurant, she did a menu dedicated to ‘If I Go’ where it was a discount, 15 percent off or something if you bought a ticket,” she said. “People understand the importance of this,” said Brooks. “If the film wasn’t good, I wouldn’t be doing all this.”.

On the awards front, the challenge is still getting the film in front of the steak eaters who still make up a good chunk of the awards body, and maybe do not immediately think they identify with the material. “The Academy is working really hard to change that narrative by who is allowed to vote. The voting party is shifting, but that’s what I’m experiencing right now,” mentioned Brooks.

Sources indicate that but regular filmgoers have a role in getting smaller, truly independent films awards recognition too. “The general audience plays a huge part because the culture tells the voters where to look, what is notable,” noted the actress. “The people, we have a voice in this too. I think we make it very clear what we want to see, but it’s a weird cycle.” Studio films have a budget for billboards, commercials, advertisements, and more. “When you are a small independent film, you have to be that massive machine on your own to get it out there. And that’s a lot of work, and that’s a lot of time, and that’s a lot of smarts,” said Brooks. “You’ve got to have a lot of faith and hope too. You’ve just got to believe that what you’ve created is strong. And I do know that we all do, myself, J. Alphonse, Walter, MACRO, Rich Spirit, we believe in this film wholeheartedly.”.

“Movies like these are worth telling, and I think they do reach who they need to reach, and they do lock in with the world on a larger scale when they’re supposed to,” noted Brooks, reflecting on the fruitful journey “If I Go” has already had so far. “This is the thing I’m most proud of in my whole career because just the fact that people are having conversations, hard conversations with their loved ones, and they’re finding ways to heal.”.

It has been revealed that to get there, however, Marvel will need to provide one of its most thrilling and memorable experiences yet with the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday and Avengers: Secret Wars. Considering the history of the franchise to date, there is one issue with the movie that Marvel may not be able to solve before its planned release date on December 17, 2027.

In a recent development, avengers: Secret Wars is still on the calendar for December 2027, but it has not yet begun principal photography. Following Doomsday's production, which shot from April to September 2025, its cast only reunited for reshoots throughout 2025 and 2026, laying the groundwork for the sequel's success.

This contrast makes Secret Wars' production that much more worrying. With only 13 months until it is set to debut in cinemas, Secret Wars has not begun filming on its enormous, high-stakes story, which is expected to see the stories of characters from multiple different universes put together in Battleworld.

While some movies are able to come together rapidly, the extensive size and scale of Secret Wars has called the release of the upcoming film into question. Especially considering the trajectory of the franchise to date, there are a few valid concerns to address concerning Secret Wars and its planned release date.

Avengers: Secret Wars is at the moment rumored to begin filming in January 2027, and if this occurs, it will have the smallest gap between production start and theatrical release of any installment in the Avengers franchise to date. The first Avengers currently holds this record with 13 months, beginning production in April 2011 for a May 2012 release.

Avengers: Age of Ultron extended this window slightly, beginning filming in February 2014 for a May 2015 wide theatrical release.

Avengers: Infinity War had a similar gap, filming in January 2017 for a theatrical release in late April, while Avengers: Endgame extended the production time significantly, beginning its production in August 2017 for release in April 2019.

Almost every Marvel movie has begun filming more than a year before release. With Secret Wars looking likely to begin photography in January, and setting a new record for the shortest time between production and release, this has naturally led to concerns about the film being done in time for its release date.

Sources indicate that avengers: Secret Wars is sure to be one of the biggest movies of 2027, packed full of all kinds of characters in all sorts of thrilling environments. A project like that takes time, and the thought of turning a satisfying film around in such a tight window is concerning.

Most significant-budget movies take a long time in post-production. Once movies are shot, they are put through a rigorous process of editing, sound design, visual effects, and rendering. These efforts are time-consuming, especially in the case of visual spectacles like the Avengers movies, which require a staggering amount of effects.

Sources indicate that beyond even the Avengers films, looking at 2026's biggest hits highlights this difficulty for Secret Wars. Project Hail Mary began filming in 2024 for its 2026 release, as did Michael. This long runway for production gives the filmmakers room to ensure the final film lives up to expectations.

Industry observers note that with all of this considered, Secret Wars is supposed to be the biggest Avengers entry yet. Giving it the least amount of time to be executed to its fullest potential is worrying, but the prospect of delaying it might be an even greater difficulty for Marvel.

Industry observers note that marvel has cleared the calendar for its Avengers films, which between Doomsday and Secret Wars, promise to reshape the entire universe. Still, there are events that are planned to come afterward, with three enormous releases set for 2028, beginning with Marvel's new reboot of the X-Men in May.

If Secret Wars is delayed, this will not only mean that the franchise will not have any films released during 2027's calendar year, but it will also likely have to push back Marvel's enormous slate. While delaying Secret Wars to February could mitigate this difficulty, that release window is not nearly as historically successful as December or summer.

Sources indicate that if Secret Wars is delayed, it will more likely be pushed back to May. If this is the case, a whole cascade of changes will likely follow. X-Men will certainly need to be pushed back from its May releaseand will likely take Ghost Rider's July slot. From there, Ghost Rider could likely find a suitable spot in the fall, allowing Black Panther 3 to still release that December.

According to recent reports, still, releasing four films in a year is a lot to ask of audiences who have already shown fatigue in some of Marvel's most jam-packed years. The ideal situation for all would be for Secret Wars to retain its release date. And while this looks increasingly less assured, it is still possible.

With all of this considered, it is still possible for Secret Wars to make its release date. If the film begins shooting in January, scheduling would be tight, but it is notable that this year's box office juggernaut Spider-Man: Brand Fresh Day had a similar gap. That film began production in early August 2025 for a late July 2026 release.

In addition, much of Secret Wars has likely already been done behind the scenes. The next Multiversal Saga film will largely be put together digitally, with many of the environments and characters rendered in visual effects throughout some of the film's action-packed events.

Filming is important, but it is also essential to note that Joe and Anthony Russo have been working on Doomsday and Secret Wars concurrently since 2024. Deep development and key visuals on both projects have been in process since that time, and certain scenes for Secret Wars could even have been captured during Doomsday's production.

Sources indicate that yes, this tight window for filming and release is a reason for concern. However, few filmmakers know how to navigate the machinations of the Marvel Cinematic Universe as well as the Russos do. Until Marvel indicates otherwise, Avengers: Secret Wars is still set for release in December 2027.

The holiday shopping season is here, and Apple Watch is always a popular gift. Apple’s lineup includes the affordable Apple Watch SE 3 and the more advanced Apple Watch Series 12.

Here’s how those two Apple Watch models stack up….

The Apple Watch SE 3 is the most affordable way to enter the Apple Watch ecosystem. It got a substantial update last year, adding a variety of new higher-end Apple Watch features. It now offers an Always-On display, sleep apnea notifications, temperature sensing, interactive wrist flick and double tap gestures, and more.

It has been revealed that the Apple Watch SE 3 offers 18 hours of battery life, though you can stretch that to 32 hours in Low Power Mode. It supports fast charging, going from 0-80% in 45 minutes.

Industry observers note that even though it hasn’t been updated in a year, the Apple Watch SE 3 is a very compelling option, especially for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem. It’s pretty fantastic that you can get an Apple Watch with key display and health-monitoring features for under $200.

Recent findings suggest that the Apple Watch Series 12 is Apple’s newest smartwatch, and it’s a significant update over its predecessor. This year, Apple doubled down on the health and fitness capabilities of Apple Watch with an all-new Health Sensing System.

Apple touts that the Apple Watch Series 12 delivers “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” In fact, the company conducted a study of more than 1,000 participants that found the Series 12 “achieved statistically better overall accuracy than every competing wearable it tested across workouts and daily activities.”.

With the newly introduced system, Apple Watch Series 12 captures your heart rate every five seconds. Previous Apple Watch models, including the Apple Watch SE 3, take measurements every five minutes. The new Health Sensing System also enables a new readiness score feature, which factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score.

As I wrote in my review, the Apple Watch Series 12 brings some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. The new sensing system unlocks a trove of new data along with better accuracy.

In a recent development, the Apple Watch lineup is incredibly strong right now. Whether you’re deciding between the SE 3 and Series 12, both offer great health tracking, battery life, and connectivity. The Apple Watch SE 3 is an excellent choice for people newly introduced to the Apple Watch ecosystem.

The Apple Watch Series 12, however, is the best Apple Watch for most people. There are major improvements to the health tracking capabilities, offering meaningful steps forward in what the Apple Watch can tell you about yourself. In the two months I’ve had mine, I’ve come to appreciate the more frequent heart rate measurement and readiness score.

Given how much of Godzilla's appeal over the last seven decades has been predicated on the big guy's ability to reduce entire cities to rubble, there's something quite amusing about the prospect of spending hours building him out of little plastic bricks. We've seen LEGO give us some wonderfully elaborate recreations of locations from our favorite movies over the years, although in this instance, it's probably best not to display your latest acquisition too close to any of those buildings. And if you've been wondering what to get the Godzilla fan in your life for Christmas, LEGO has come up with something that should keep them occupied well into the new year.

As of today, November 27, you can get your hands on LEGO's 5,363-piece Godzilla set for $449.99, exclusively through the LEGO Store. Based on the version of Godzilla we've seen in the MonsterVerse movies, the finished model stands more than 27.5 inches tall, and there are a few different ways you can pose him once you've put him together. You can even have him firing his atomic breath, while everything from his tail to his individual fingers can be repositioned.

Sources indicate that what's particularly impressive about the design is the amount of detail that's gone into recreating Godzilla's scales, given that so much of the creature is essentially the same color. The blue dorsal plates running all the way down his back and along his tail give the model a little more color, and if you'd prefer to have Godzilla on display without his atomic breath, you can replace the piece protruding from his mouth with a red tongue. The set is designed for builders aged 18 and over.

Industry observers note that as has become something of a tradition with LEGO's major Black Friday releases, there's an additional set available to those who purchase Godzilla over the course of the holiday weekend. The 359-piece Godzilla Logo & Footprint set is available as a gift with purchase between November 27 and November 30, while supplies last. Designed to be displayed alongside the considerably larger Godzilla model, the accompanying set won't be available to purchase separately.

Of course, given that Godzilla himself measures more than two feet tall, 10.5 inches wide, and 15.5 inches long, prospective buyers might want to spend a little time figuring out where they're going to put him before they start building. Between the two sets, those who manage to get their hands on the Black Friday exclusive will have a combined 5,722 pieces to work their way through over Christmas.

#155662. ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down

‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2065 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • [Editor’s Note: The following review contains spoilers for “The Lowdown” Season 2 Episode 8, “The Tower” — including the finale’s ending.].
  • “I saw the structure of the episode as these kind of waves that crash upon Lee,” Ethan Hawke remarked in an interview about “The Lowdown‘s” Season 2 finale.
  • Industry observers note that lee’s walls were certainly up when “The Lowdown” Season 2 began.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s Note: The following review contains spoilers for “The Lowdown” Season 2 Episode 8, “The Tower” — including the finale’s ending.].

“I saw the structure of the episode as these kind of waves that crash upon Lee,” Ethan Hawke remarked in an interview about “The Lowdown‘s” Season 2 finale. “The way life works, it’s not like, ‘Oh, this one thing happens and then you change.’ It’s usually a series of things that happen, and the walls of your defenses come down.”.

Industry observers note that lee’s walls were certainly up when “The Lowdown” Season 2 began. Untethered by the acclaim for his Season 1 exposé on Dale Washberg (Tim Blake Nelson), Lee reacts with vehement defensiveness. He mocks the journalists who named him Tulsa’s Journalist of the Year during his acceptance speech. He alienates his friends and embarrasses his daughter. Related Stories ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It.

He’s a mess, and when Ginger (Betty Gilpin) walks into his life with a tantalizing upcoming story, he’s lucky — not because she’s the woman of his dreams carrying his drug of choice (a “truthstorian’s” next crusade), but because grounding forces are on the way in the form of his estranged father, Lee Raybon Sr. (Tommy Lee Jones), as well as a few clear-eyed, full-throated friends. Over the course of a riveting, revelatory Season 2, they all help to bring Lee back to himself, one wave at a time.

Industry observers note that the finale’s first swell comes as quite a surprise — two surprises, really. When Lee pulls up to the funeral home, prepared to pay a terse goodbye to his departed dad, so, too, does his former business partner and best friend, Wendell (played by Peter Dinklage). Wendell tells Lee he’ll “always be grateful” for Senior’s guidance when they were younger, and it’s immediately clear he’s not about to take the man’s final tribute as lightly as his son may have hoped.

Industry observers note that “When Tommy’s character dies and there’s a funeral, we’re all like, ‘Well, wouldn’t Wendell be there?’ I mean, they’re really great friends,'” Hawke stated. “I called Peter up and I was like, ‘Is there any way you’d come down for one day to be just at this funeral?’ And Peter was shooting in London and flew in and flew right back. He came in and made it happen for us.”.

But Dinklage’s return was no mere cameo. Creator Sterlin Harjo knew better than to let the opportunity go to waste.

It has been revealed that “I think there was a Shakespeare monologue in it first, and it was beautiful,” Harjo said. “Then Peter suggested the Dylan Thomas. […] I can’t imagine a more exciting way to have Peter be in your show than doing this Dylan Thomas poem that’s a gentle poem, but he does it with this rage — how it’s supposed to be read. It’s amazing.”.

In a recent development, volunteering to speak when Ray (Michael Hitchcock) gets overwhelmed, Wendell spends a few seconds scrolling to find the right poem (“Do not go gentle into that good night”) and then tears into it with vigor. Dinklage’s recitation is more of a resuscitation — powerful enough to wake the dead, it wakes Lee up, snapping him into the present and bringing him back to life.

In a recent development, “When he’s doing the poem, he came in at a 10,” Harjo noted. “The only direction I gave him was, ‘What if you build to that?’ And that’s what he did, and it was just unbelievably great.”.

“That one is violent and abrupt,” Hawke remarked. “It’s a friend shaking you up.”.

In a recent development, in Hawke’s case, Lee’s friend was his real friend. He knew Dinklage “loved poetry,” and he even knew a little bit about what his fellow actor would bring to this poem.

“This is where collaboration is really mysterious about how it works and when it works really well,” Hawke said. “I’ve been friends with Peter Dinklage since, I don’t know, 1990. […] We both arrived in Fresh York around the same time, and we used to sit around and tie one on and try to flirt with girls and read poems. We used to geek out about how much we loved the ways people would read poems in the old days. If you hear Dylan Thomas read a poem or you hear Orson Wells read a poem, they weren’t afraid of feeling or emotion or a theatricality. They weren’t afraid of passion — actual passion — and caring and looking foolish.”.

In a recent development, “We’re living in an age of irony and cynicism and detachment, and this definition of cool being that you don’t care. Whereas the definition when I was growing up was Bob Marley and John Lennon and Miles Davis and those guys cared a tremendous amount. They weren’t detached. They were completely attached. So for me to watch Peter bring that to his performance was like, ‘Let me show you kids how to do a poem!’ [laughs] ‘You got to do it like your life depends on it.'”.

It has been revealed that “The key to that scene is the interaction between him and Lee,” Harjo said. “I love that he’s watching Lee the whole time. It’s like there’s no one else in the room and he’s doing it for Lee. I love that.”.

According to recent reports, “The camera does pick up subconscious,” Hawke noted. “A lot of times I’ll see work that might be good, but it has no subconscious to it. I can tell there’s no secret sewn into the filmmaking. And Sterlin loves — you can call it poetry, you can call it whatever you want — but [he loves] when there’s multiple layers happening. […] And so for me, I’m not just sitting there with an actor doing this scene. I’ve known this guy for 30 years and I know what this poem means to him, and he knows me.”.

“If there was an Academy Award for Best Single Scene, I would give it to Peter Dinklage in our show.”.

While Dinklage may have to settle for an Emmy, Harjo had to write the other major finale monologue for an actual Oscar winner. At the reception, Lee’s daughter Francis (Ryan Kiera Armstrong) reads a passage from her grandfather’s journal, written shortly after Lee Jr. was born, as a way to honor her ancestor. Then, as Francis speaks Senior’s words, Senior appears seated behind her, and Tommy Lee Jones takes over the scene.

“The bigger thing about that monologue is I knew it was coming,” Harjo stated. “I was like, ‘Oh shit, I got to write this thing for Tommy Lee Jones.’ I kind of had Tommy Lee Jones dialed in through the whole season. I felt like I could really write his voice. But when it came to that monologue, I’m like, ‘God, he’s already known for one of the best monologues in the world at the end of ‘No Country for Old Men,’ and I can either try to do a fancy monologue that isn’t like that at all, or I could lean into the fact that Cormac McCarthy and the Coen brothers did this really well already, and there’s no way that I don’t know that as a filmmaker. So I’m going to lean into it and almost give homage to that speech.'”.

In a recent development, “And that’s what I did. It has this bit of nostalgia. It also has this magic to it and this dreamlike quality to what he’s doing,” Harjo stated. “The character is such an internal person that the only way you’re going to get those monologues is through a journal when he thinks it’s the privacy of himself and his journal. He’s expressing things that he wouldn’t normally express out loud.”.

It has been revealed that “Not to toot my own horn, but I feel like I nailed it,” he said, laughing. “Of course, it filters through Tommy Lee Jones and all of a sudden it’s like this fucking amazing thing that he does. It was wonderful being on set. Just watching him give that, it was unbelievable. I could have used any take and it would’ve been amazing in a different way.”.

Sources indicate that throughout the monologue, Lee sits in thoughtful silence. He’s not only absorbing what his father wrote and remembering who he was; he’s also recognizing his shifting role as a son who’s now a father. There’s a connection across generations. Yes, his responsibility to his daughter means avoiding repeating his dad’s mistakes, which Lee is well-aware of, but it also means honoring his father’s better intentions, like the ones he voiced in that journal and Francis is voicing again now.

Recent findings suggest that “Lee’s adamant that he’s nothing like his father,” Hawke remarked. “The first thought I had is, ‘All right, this is why Lee Raybon is obsessed with the truth: It’s that his father was a chronic liar.’ If you grew up in a house where your parent was really comfortable lying to you, you would get obsessed with people in power misleading you, and that would really drive you.”.

Recent findings suggest that “But then as we played the scenes deeper, I realized that Lee was lying to himself; that he was just as manipulative as his father is. He just does it in the name of truth. All this bad behavior that he was in denial of, he’d actually internalized it, and he was so much like his dad that he was completely blind to it, which is behavior I’ve seen in so many friends. It’s amazing. But I had to live through it. I didn’t get it when I was reading it. I got it when I was playing it, and that was very powerful for me.”.

One way Harjo & co. illustrate Lee’s development over the course of Season 2 is simple: He listens. Instead of shouting, pontificating, or generally causing chaos, Lee spends much of the finale hearing what everyone around him has to say. Even when he’s up his own ass or annoying the hell out of folks, he has a community who cares about him, and their steady presence in his life is what eventually breaks down his defenses.

Industry observers note that “The first [wave] is Peter reading that poem, and then the second one is gentle and persuasive where my daughter is revealing to me that my father did love me,” Hawke remarked. “Part of the thing you learn watching this show is that Lee feels like he has to conquer the world to be worthy of self-respect. His daughter is saying, ‘It’s right here for you, and it always has been.'”.

Recent findings suggest that while another monologue played a significant role in how the episode plays out — Ginger’s speech to Francis, outside the bookstore — that moment wasn’t about Lee. (“The whole idea was Ginger and Francis don’t really get to hang out, but they are alike,” Harjo stated. “Ginger immediately recognizes it and probably also knows that she had a father that was a lot like Lee.”) So his final wave comes from a curious source.

Recent findings suggest that “The third one is just this final little moment that happens with Vickey (Abbie Cobb) when she tells him his fortune is bad and he sees it as a good thing. He understands that everything is point of view, and for him, towers coming down would be good.”.

“Those are the three steps that I think are designed to get Lee back on his feet again,” Hawke said. “That push him to be like, ‘All right, you know what? I’m not quitting. I’m going to keep being me, and I’m going to be a better version of me.'”.

Industry observers note that how he’s feeling when Season 3 starts is anyone’s guess, and that assumes a renewal that’s yet to be declared is still in the offing from FX. But one thing’s for sure: If Lee comes back, he’ll be a changed man — and he won’t be alone.

“The Lowdown” is available on FX and Hulu.

Sources indicate that one of the best features in The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered is the ability to use mods across all available platforms. CD Projekt Red included a fair number of popular mods when the Remastered version rolled out at the end of September, but console players had far fewer options than PC players. CD Projekt Red is looking to bridge that gap with a new revision.

CD Projekt Red released patch 5.02 on Nov. 26 across Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X. According to recent reports, [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published on April 24, 2026, when “I Swear” was released in American theaters. Aramayo recently won Best Actor in a Film at the BAFTA Scotland Awards. The film and his performance are eligible for this year’s Oscars, and “I Swear” is now streaming on Netflix.].

When Robert Aramayo signed on to play Scottish Tourette’s activist John Davidson in filmmaker Kirk Jones’ biopic “I Swear,” he could scarcely imagine where the film would take him.

Industry observers note that A hit in the UK, the film netted Aramayo a pair of BAFTA wins earlier in the year, as the British actor won both the vaunted Rising Star Award (previous winners include James McAvoy, John Boyega, Tom Holland, Tom Hardy, and those are just some of its biggest names) and the Best Actor trophy (beating out Timothée Chalamet, Leonardo DiCaprio, Ethan Hawke, Jesse Plemons, and eventual Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan). Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

In a recent development, but that’s hardly all that happened at the February awards show, which was instantly and forever marred by a number of loud, racist outbursts from Davidson himself that were directed at “Sinners” stars Jordan, Delroy Lindo, Wunmi Mosaku, and more. The fallout from the incident was both swift and prolonged, and will likely impact the domestic release of “I Swear,” which is rolling out in stateside theaters now.

Aramayo’s performance in the film is indeed star-making and awards-worthy, as he brings sensitivity and great courage to his portrayal of Davidson, following him from his earliest symptoms through his current passionate activism. Hopefully, viewers can see and appreciate the work on its own merits, and get to know Aramayo much better, though he has previously appeared in plenty of projects recognizable to American audiences, from “The Empty Man” to “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” to a little thing called “Game of Thrones” (young Ned Stark!).

Ahead, Aramayo tells IndieWire about his deep research for the role, everything BAFTAs, and what he hopes will come from more people seeing the film and, hopefully, understanding Tourette’s all the better.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: When I saw the film at TIFF in September, I did my due diligence before I reviewed it, and learned that John is a huge figure in the UK, but relatively unknown in America. How much did you know about him before this film?

It has been revealed that robert Aramayo: John’s made a lot of documentaries, but the massive one that probably had the most impact was “John’s Not Mad,” and that was in 1989. So if you speak to people who were around then, they have a lot of very personal stories about watching that documentary and being like, “Wow, is this Tourette’s? What’s Tourette’s?”.

So when you get the script, are you someone who then wants to do more research into him, or do you feel like the script is the thing?

It has been revealed that the production team and Kirk were so gracious, and they gave me so much time. I think they were like, “Oh, yeah, take a couple of months or something to research and stuff.” I was really thankful for that. The first thing that I did was to meet John; I met him very quickly. And then I went away for a month, and I spent that time gaining as much knowledge as I could about Tourette’s and what it is. That was through watching the documentaries, watching YouTube videos, and reading books.

I based myself in Galashiels and spent weeks with John, just following him around and spending as much time with him as I could. And also traveling through Scotland, meeting people, mainly through [support organization] Tourette Scotland, who lived with Tourette’s as well. I wanted to have, I don’t know, a more expansive view of Tourette’s than just John. Obviously, John was my main focus, though.

It has been revealed that when you’re getting ready to meet John, what were you expecting and anticipating? What were you nervous about?

I don’t know what I felt, really. I was so filled with anxiety about, oh my word, am I going to do this? I wanted John to like me. I was already feeling, God, this is going to be a really big challenge. And I met him within days of saying yes.

But then, when I met him, one thing that struck me straight away was his knowledge. He’s got a really amazing knowledge about, obviously, Tourette’s, but also a lot of neurodiversity and how it lives, other conditions that exist with Tourette’s, and stuff like that. He’s got a lot of thoughts about how we can do better and help young people and things like that. He’s very forthcoming with it.

He’s got so much heart. He’s such an amazing, welcoming, supportive man that I was just like, wow, this is a really impressive person that I’m meeting here. Of course, then your anxiety and the responsibility meter have gone through the roof.

Just watching the film, I learned so much about what Tourette’s can entail and the very wide spectrum of symptoms that people can have. What was the most unexpected thing you learned about it during your research?

A couple of things really that had a really big impact on me straight away, and that sort of broke my perception of what I thought Tourette’s was, that anything can be a tic, and that it’s so singular to the person. So if you’ve met one person with Tourette’s, someone noted to me, you’ve met one person with Tourette’s. That was a big thing.

Recent findings suggest that and also the fact that there’s a lot of tics that you just don’t see. There’s tics that you don’t see as tics because anything can be a tic, or there’s tics that exist only in somebody’s mind, and things like that, tics linked with OCD. Just the complexity of it was massive.

It has been revealed that I learned some statistics recently, which I found really interesting: One in 50 kids in America live with persistent tic disorder, and one in 160 live with Tourette’s, so it’s unbelievably common, it’s everywhere. We have met people with Tourette’s, we meet them all the time. It was part of the experience of the film as well, we met loads of people who were living with Tourette’s undiagnosed. 50 percent of people who live with Tourette’s in the U.S. are undiagnosed, and that was true for us in the UK as well in our experience. Maybe the thing is that we don’t know that that’s what’s happening. That made me think, wow, there’s a real educational piece to this as well.

According to recent reports, you are playing someone who is a real person who has been captured on film for many years. People know what he looks like, they know what he sounds like. How do you find the line between impersonation and impression in your performance?

I never wanted to impersonate John. I think I would’ve gone the wrong way if that was what I was thinking. You have to, at a certain point, take ownership of the character and try and make him your own. I was lucky because there was so much that I needed to learn, so for so long, I wasn’t thinking about performance or playing him at all. I was just trying to immerse myself as much as I could in everything, anything that I could get my hands on. Then, at certain point, I moved to thinking about how I was going to try and play my version of John.

In a [narrative] film, you get the opportunity to maybe show a little bit more [than a documentary]. A documentary film crew comes into somebody’s life and they can capture what they can capture, but we could capture way more intimate moments throughout the whole film that John had spoken to.

We could show the moments where he is on his own, whether there’s been an impact or how he’s feeling or his emotional life, how things change over time and stuff like that, and hopefully try and do it with truth and authenticity.

You attended Juilliard, which always seems a little, “Oooohhh, he’s Juilliard-trained.”.

But now that you’re a few years out of school, what are the pieces of training that are proving to be most useful to you?

I think that acting teachers and drama school is vocabulary, really. At the time, certain things that teachers would say to me had a massive impact on me and really opened me up to other ways of looking at things, and other things are only impacting me now, as I keep working and as I get older. I think that’s the beauty of drama school, you get flooded with all of this stuff, and then you’re going, “Oh, that’s what they were talking about.” And then there’s things that my teachers would consistently say, “You’ve got to work on this, you’ve got to work on this,” and I’m still working on it. It’s like a toolbox, and every now and again you go, “Oh, yeah, that’s what I need.”.

They also made us do liberal arts which — I’m from Yorkshire, I don’t even know what liberal arts meant — but I’d encounter Nietzsche and Plato and all this stuff. I had no time at all to digest anything, but I’d read it and be like, “I don’t really know what’s going on here, but I think this is going to be important one day. I think I’m going to reread this one day!”.

What was the morning of the BAFTA nominations like for you?

Sources indicate that I knew it was happening that morning. I remember talking to my agent, and we just didn’t speak about it, but we both knew that they were coming out that morning or whatever, so we had a really chill conversation about something else. [Laughs] I put it on in the background, because I thought we had a chance at, I don’t know, something, and then I heard that Peter had been nominated and I was so happy for him. I was elated for him.

It has been revealed that so, I was just in that, and I was doing the dishes, and I was like, “Wow, that’s so cool. I can’t wait to go text him.” And then they stated my name, and I just absolutely couldn’t believe it. My agent called me back straight away and was like, “Oh, my God.” It was an amazing feeling, but it was really unexpected because I was still really, really sort of overwhelmed by the Rising Star thing.

You genuinely looked so surprised when you won Best Actor at the show. I feel like I would black out in that moment. Do you remember what that moment felt like?

Yeah, because I almost did! I had this weird physical reaction where I sort of went back [pantomimes sitting way back], and I think somebody grabbed me. I think I would’ve just kept going. I would’ve fallen off my chair or something.

I honestly couldn’t believe it. I’m honestly not sure I still can believe that that’s something that happened to me, because for someone like me to be in that group of people blew my mind. I felt like, “Wow, and there I am, that’s my name.” To me, that was the thing that sort of really, really, really, really blew me away. When it happened, yes, it all just becomes a blur, and I’m running down the stairs, and I don’t know what the hell I’m going to say.

According to recent reports, obviously, other things happened at the awards show involving John. As someone who had seen the film, I felt like I had a greater grasp on what was happening; I had that context. Now that the film is coming out in America, what hopes do you have for people seeing the film and how that might impact that conversation?

I think lots of people watch the film, and they feel like their education around Tourette’s has improved and increased, and that would be amazing [if that continued]. I think it’s vital to acknowledge that … Tourette’s has an impact on a person who’s ticcing, and the same tic obviously has an impact on the person who’s receiving the tic or impacted by the tic. And it’s important to acknowledge that, because that is what it is. Coprolalia, which is the tic that John has, that tic, it’s not saying what you think, it’s saying the worst thing imaginable. That’s how it was described to me.

Industry observers note that I hope people watch the film. And I hope people watch the film and think, “Oh, I’ve learned something about Tourette’s.” I hope that people watch the film from the community, because that’s been an amazing thing as well. People watching it who have lived with Tourette’s or lived with another neurodiverse condition have reached out and noted, “I see myself in this.” You want people to go to the movies and enjoy the film, but if people go home and Google “John Davidson” or Google “Tourette’s,” that’d be amazing.

It has been revealed that the film is going to introduce you to a much larger audience, but you’ve also been in some massive hits before this one. Which is a fun way to ask: Do you know that “The Empty Man” has a huge cult fandom?

[Laughs] I’ve been told this. What an experience. I loved making that film. It was a long journey with it, and I learned a lot. And it was my first movie that I’d done with James Badge Dale, and I did another one with him as well. And I really, really liked working with him. He’s a really nice guy, and he’s a really talented actor. And the director, David [Prior], was wonderful. I learned a lot on that film. I love that people love that film.

In a recent development, you are also in the “Lord of the Rings” world as well. Are you going to be turning out to see “The Hunt for Gollum”?

According to recent reports, I’m so excited. I can’t wait. I’m a massive fan of the Peter Jackson films. I can’t wait to see what they do with it. It’s a really interesting story. I’m glad that they’re doing it and doing it properly.

Now that you’ve had what feels like a big breakthrough, what sort of things are you pursuing next?

Recent findings suggest that what do I want to do next? I don’t know! I feel lucky to just be an actor, to work. I’ve been lucky enough to work with some incredible people on “I Swear,” to work with Kirk and Peter and Shirley and Maxine. People like that, you learn, you grow, you get better. And so if I can just keep doing it, I’ll be happy.

That Rising Star Award feels like a lot of pressure!

I just feel really, really grateful for everyone who voted for me. It’s such a cool award that the public, the British public, vote for you. I feel so grateful for everyone who voted for me. I just feel very, very grateful for the whole thing, for everything, and mainly that people hopefully watch the film and talk about it.

For more information about Tourette Syndrome and access to free resources and support, visit the Tourette Association of America right here.

  • It has been revealed that netflix has taken shots at a variety of genres and storytelling styles, sometimes hitting it out of the park but missing badly on other occasions.
  • It has been revealed that one of its best is also one of the streamer's best science fiction shows, Love, Death & Robots.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Netflix's four-season science fiction TV series is great from start to finish, and even its weakest episode is miles better than the sci-fi shows you'll find on other streamers. Netflix's sci-fi offerings are not quite at the level of a streaming app like Apple TV, with its huge library of great shows in the genre, but it still has some winners.

It has been revealed that netflix has taken shots at a variety of genres and storytelling styles, sometimes hitting it out of the park but missing badly on other occasions. It has managed to carve out one niche, though, and that's with anthologies. Black Mirror, Guillermo del Toro's Cabinet of Curiosities, and Beef are all celebrated anthologies.

It has been revealed that one of its best is also one of the streamer's best science fiction shows, Love, Death & Robots. The four-season, 45-episode anthology series consists of 6–21 minute shorts, all animated and written by different creative teams, with a handful of groups double-dipping over the seasons.

The only thing uniting the stories, save for the occasional multi-parter, is that they each deal with one of the themes of the title, and often deal with more than one. Love, Death & Robots premiered in 2019, and has had such illustrious directors as David Fincher craft their own episodes.

With 45 episodes, you would think that more than a handful wouldn't make the grade, but Love, Death & Robots is one of the rare shows where every episode is worth watching. There are certainly some that are worse than others, but even the least of them stands up to the best other sci-fi shows can offer.

The worst episode of Love, Death & Robots is probably not objective, considering how unique each episode is, and how varying animation styles, tones, and subject matter will appeal to everyone differently. However, a good case can be made for "Life Hutch" being the worst. Then again, another case can be made for it still being very watchable.

In a recent development, season 2, episode 7, is "Life Hutch", an episode that uses photorealistic animation and stars Michael B. Jordan as Terence, a space pilot who gets stranded on a desolate planet and fights a murderous robot. Jordan could certainly have been used better, and the flashbacks take up too much time that a short episode simply doesn't have to spare.

However, there's still a lot going for it, including the animation that will have you wondering if everything is actually live-action with a few CGI touch-ups here and there. Jordan may be underused, but even a little Jordan is better than no Jordan. "Hutch" probably ranks low on most people's "best of" Love, Death & Robots lists, but that doesn't mean they're skipping it.

Recent findings suggest that love, Death & Robots makes every episode of the series watchable by giving each creative team total freedom to tell their story. If someone wants to make a classic sci-fi tale of mech-suits fighting alien invaders, they are free to. If they want to put on a Red Hot Chili Peppers concert with characters designed like marionettes, they can do that too.

Industry observers note that there's a lot of freedom on display in Love, Death & Robots, and even the episodes that don't work as well still showcase creators putting exactly what they want on screen. You don't sense an invisible hand guiding the Love, Death & Robots episodes; it's a show for animators and writers as much as it is for the audience.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if any genre has benefited from a massive resurgence, it’s the Western.
  • From a Yellowstone prequel to the greatest rivalry in American history, these six series are perfect to wet your Western whistle.
  • According to recent reports, the last decade of television has been dominated by Taylor Sheridan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if any genre has benefited from a massive resurgence, it’s the Western. The 21st century has watched the genre boom as newfound stories have been told. Whether it be period dramas or neo-Westerns, audiences have flocked to watch. If you’re seeking a Western show during a free weekend, we have six bingeable Western demonstrates you can finish in a day or two.

From a Yellowstone prequel to the greatest rivalry in American history, these six series are perfect to wet your Western whistle. These highlights range from brutal depictions of the wild frontier to daring tales of a journey toward new hope; they capture the full gamut of Western narratives. Though there are some incredible long-running Western shows, their runtime would exceed the weekend allotment. So, whip out your Stetson and turn on these six shows for a wonderful weekend watch!

According to recent reports, the last decade of television has been dominated by Taylor Sheridan. Audiences were immediately taken by Yellowstone and the Dutton dynasty that the visionary found the opportunity to expand the story through a self-contained prequel, 1883. The Western drama follows the post-Civil War Dutton family as they flee poverty in Texas and embark on a perilous journey west across the Great Plains. Guided by tough Pinkerton agents Shea Brennan (Sam Elliott) and Thomas (LaMonica Garrett) alongside a caravan of inexperienced European immigrants, James and Margaret Dutton (Tim McGraw and Faith Hill) face ruthless bandits, treacherous river crossings, and harsh frontier conditions. Their grueling trek toward the untamed American frontier ultimately leads them to settle in Montana, establishing the roots of what will become the Yellowstone Ranch. 1883 pairs a tough survival story with gritty frontier realism, high-stakes emotion, and visual wonder for an extraordinary period series.

What makes 1883 work is that it tells a complete story through a stellar 10-hour journey. Every river crossing, illness, and weather shift carries immediate consequences for survival. 1883 refuses to sanitize the journey, adopting a gritty tone that emphasizes physical hardship, loss, and lingering post-Civil War trauma. Filmed across Texas and Montana locations with a sweeping musical score, the miniseries captures expansive landscapes and intimate character moments on a film-like scale. Elliott anchors the story, bringing his classical Western flair to the screen. Hill and McGraw bring natural chemistry that carries great emotional weight. Isabel May delivers the best performance as Elsa Dutton, whose profound narration frames the trail's harshness and wonder. With only ten episodes, 1883 is easily achievable. While the story is tied to the greater Yellowstone universe, there’s no necessary baggage attached to watching. 1883 is an easy gateway into Sheridan’s longer-running indicates.

I’ll preface this now: American Primeval is absolutely not for the faint of heart. That remarked, it’s a truly fascinating story. Created by Mark L. Smith and directed by Peter Berg, the six-episode series follows a mother, Sara Rowell (Betty Gilpin), and her young son, Devin (Preston Mota), as they flee their past and cross the unforgiving frontier to reunite with her husband. With the help of a reluctant, Shoshone-raised tracker named Isaac Reed (Taylor Kitsch), they form an unlikely found family while fighting to survive violent clashes among Mormon militias, Indigenous tribes, fur trappers, and the U.S. Army. Loosely inspired by real historical events like the Mountain Meadows Massacre, American Primeval explores the bloody collision of culture, religion, and survival at the birth of the American West. The gritty, gripping drama pairs a brutal survival story with a bleak, lawless vision of the 1857 Utah Territory that unabashedly leans into brutal realism, clashing factions, and visceral tension.

American Primeval is unlike the romanticized Westerns you’ve seen before. The narrative pits Indigenous tribes, Mormon militias, fur trappers, settlers, and the U.S. Army against one another, exploring power, land, and religious conflict. With authentic craft and atmosphere, outdoor filming in New Mexico, period-style set work, a score by Explosions in the Sky, and Indigenous cultural and language consultation give the series a stark, grounded feel. The series explores the Church of Latter-day Saints in a fascinating way, presenting Bingham Young (Kim Coates) as tyrannical and raising concerns about its portrayal. Yet, tackling the Mountain Meadows Massacre is a bold risk well worth taking. American Primeval is a harrowing drama that is a truly sensational production. It's violent, but that’s what the West was.

Female-focused Westerns are rare, so when they arrive, it’s notable to celebrate them. Godless is a diamond-in-the-rough drama, written and directed by Scott Frank. Set in the 1880s American West, the Netflix miniseries follows ruthless outlaw Frank Griffin (Jeff Daniels) as he hunts down his former protégé, Roy Goode (Jack O’Connell), after Roy betrays his gang. On the run, Roy seeks refuge on the ranch of a hardened widow named Alice Fletcher (Michelle Dockery) in La Belle, New Mexico—an isolated mining town populated almost entirely by women after a tragic mining disaster killed the local men. When word arrives that Griffin and his murderous gang are heading their way, the women of La Belle must band together to defend their town. Godless stands out as a stellar Western by pairing classic genre scale and gritty gunplay with a fascinating female-led frontier narrative.

The seven-episode structure gives the story the space it needs to unfold. Frank allows character tensions to grow before building toward a large-scale showdown without dragging out across multiple seasons. Shot on expansive Fresh Mexico locations with wide frontier vistas and paired with Carlos Rafael Rivera's score, it balances quiet character moments with tense, violent action. With Dockery and Merritt Wever leading the charge, La Belle emerges as a brilliantly immersive Western hamlet. Daniels brings chilling unpredictability to ruthless outlaw leader Frank Griffin. Alongside Scoot McNairy, Thomas Brodie-Sangster, and Sam Waterston, Godless is a brilliantly performed series. With a visceral atmosphere and extraordinary characters, Godless was well ahead of its time.

Sports fans may debate this, but no rivalry has ever been bigger than the Hatfields and McCoys. Thankfully their story was brought to life in Hatfields & McCoys. The three-part History Channel miniseries chronicles the infamous, decades-long blood feud between two neighboring families along the West Virginia–Kentucky border. Starring Kevin Costner as patriarch Devil Anse Hatfield and Bill Paxton as his former Civil War comrade Randall McCoy, the story shows how lingering wartime bitterness, a dispute over a stolen pig, and a forbidden romance spiral into retaliatory violence. As the deadly cycle of vengeance escalates, the conflict draws in neighbors, state governors, and the U.S. Supreme Court, bringing the two states to the brink of war. Hatfields & McCoys captures the intense family-feud drama through a gritty post-Civil War setting in a tight, high-stakes story.

Sources indicate that across roughly five hours, Hatfields & McCoys tracks a real-world blood feud sparked by wartime fractures, property and livestock disputes, and a forbidden romance, showing how family loyalty and lawlessness collide. The series masters atmosphere and precise period detail with raw costumes, frontier tension, and the brutal toll of escalating reprisals. Costner and Paxton are brilliant leads, but the entire ensemble is exceptional, namely Tom Berenger, Powers Boothe, Boyd Holbrook, Jena Malone, and Mare Winningham. Though it covers about 30 years of the blood feud, the narrative wraps up cleanly by the end of the third part without leaving cliffhangers for future seasons. It’s a strong and concise narrative. If you love this real-life story, Hatfields & McCoys is the best depiction of the original family drama saga.

Recent findings suggest that four icons and four completely different ways of walking into trouble. This is the one you would have been out there, why it fits, and what it would have cost you.

You have never explained yourself and you have never needed to, because people work out fairly quickly that you are the most capable person in the room without you ever having to mention it.

You are the funniest person in most rooms and the most loyal person in all of them, and you would be genuinely insulted if somebody suggested those two things were in any tension.

You never wanted this job, and you took it anyway because the alternative was standing there watching somebody less careful do it badly, which is the most Western reason there has ever been.

Nobody has ever successfully talked you out of something you had already decided was right, and a long line of grown adults has found that out the hard way.

The Western miniseries truly began with Lonesome Dove. Directed by Simon Wincer, the adaptation of Larry McMurtry’s epic novel follows retired Texas Rangers Augustus "Gus" McCrae (Robert Duvall) and Woodrow F. Call (Tommy Lee Jones) as they leave their quiet border town to lead an ambitious cattle drive north to Montana. Inspired by an old friend's tales of untamed ranching opportunities, the duo gathers a crew of local townspeople to embark on a perilous journey across the changing American frontier. Along the way, treacherous terrain, harsh weather, violent outlaws, and personal heartbreak test their enduring friendship and resilience. Lonesome Dove faithfully captures the spirit of the Pulitzer Prize-winning story with gritty realism, deep character studies, and movie-scale production.

It has been revealed that lonesome Dove depicts the harsh Western terrain through an exploration of aging, regret, unrequited love, and the fading of the frontier. The tragedy of a changing time captures the duo as they embark on the unvarnished frontier, experiencing brutal weather, sudden danger, worn settings, and flawed individuals just trying to survive. The story thrives on McCrae and Call’s decades-long friendship and banter, which form the emotional core. Duvall and Jones are phenomenal, leading an all-star ensemble including Danny Glover, Diane Lane, Angelica Houston, and Chris Cooper. Filmed on location across Texas and Latest Mexico with a 90-day shoot and a large crew of livestock and extras, Lonesome Dove carries the weight of a blockbuster feature. While it is a product of the era, the pacing may be slower than some modern-made Westerns; Lonesome Dove’s authenticity is its greatest attribute.

Written and directed by Hugo Blick, the revisionist Western The English is a daring story. Set in 1890, the story follows Lady Cornelia Locke (Emily Blunt), an aristocratic Englishwoman who travels to the American frontier to take revenge on the man she holds responsible for her son's death. Along the way, she forms an unlikely alliance with Eli Whipp (Chaske Spencer), a retired Pawnee cavalry scout attempting to claim the ancestral land promised to him for his military service. As they journey north through a violent, lawless landscape toward Hoxem, Wyoming, they uncover a shared, tragic history that binds their fates. The English is a sweeping story that uses classic frontier visuals and a revenge-driven plot with complex individuals, cultural weight, and sharp genre subversions.

Rather than centering a traditional lone gunslinger, the series builds its story around an outsider aristocrat and an Indigenous protagonist as they navigate violence, identity, and survival on the frontier. The English subverts Western tropes and ideals by diving deep into an examination of greed, racism, land dispossession, and colonial violence. Avoiding a romanticized take, Blick tackles it head-on, letting the narrative earn its own distinct identity. The production worked with IllumiNative and specialists in Pawnee and Cheyenne history to inform its portrayal of Indigenous life and history. This cultural consultation makes the narrative richer and more authentic. Visually, the series uses saturated colors, wide landscapes, dramatic silhouettes, and torn-paper opening titles that pay homage to the Old West. A gritty and unpredictable story, it balances melancholic drama and dark humor with brutal frontier violence and interlocking mysteries. Blunt is at the top of her game. Her dynamic bond with Spencer anchors the story. At only six solid episodes, The English plays like a continuous, cohesive narrative that has room to breathe. Because the violence and bleak themes of the late 19th-century West can be intense, a weekend gives you natural breaks between episodes without needing weeks to finish.
